q: Which aromas are typical of Sauvignon Blanc?
Sauvignon Blanc is green and zesty: gooseberry, grass, nettle and citrus, with high acidity. It is rarely oaked.
Lychee and rose petals on the nose point to which white grape?
Gewürztraminer is the most perfumed classic white: lychee, rose and sweet spice. Alsace is its best-known home.
Which white grape often develops a petrol note after some years in bottle?
The petrol note is a classic sign of mature Riesling, not a fault. It comes with lime, honey and toast.
The hallmark of Riesling on the palate is…
Low acidity and an oily feel
A creamy, buttery texture from oak
Riesling keeps its acidity even when the grapes are very ripe, so even its sweet wines feel fresh, never heavy.
A young dry Riesling typically smells of…
Lime, green apple and white flowers
Young Riesling is pure fruit: lime, green apple, white peach, blossom. It is almost never aged in new oak.
A guest says “all Riesling is sweet”. What is true?
It ranges from bone-dry to very sweet
It is always sweet: it cannot be made dry
It is always bone-dry, never sweet
It is sweet only if it is aged in oak
Many of the finest Rieslings are dry. On a German label, “trocken” means dry.
Which notes are typical of an oak-aged Chardonnay?
Vanilla and toast come from the barrel, the buttery note from malolactic fermentation: the rich, round style.
An unoaked Chardonnay from a cool climate tastes of…
Green apple, lemon and wet stone
This is the Chablis style: lean, crisp and mineral, a world away from rich, oaky Chardonnay.
Chardonnay from a warm climate tends to show…
Lean green apple and steely lemon
The warmer the vineyard, the riper the fruit: apple and citrus in cool places, peach and tropical fruit in warm ones.
Why is Chardonnay often called a “winemaker’s grape”?
It is fairly neutral, so technique shapes it
It is so aromatic that it needs no oak
It grows in only one region of France
It is always blended with other grapes
Chardonnay takes the stamp of oak, lees and climate: it can be lean and steely or rich and buttery.
A guest wants a full, soft white that smells of apricot and blossom. Which grape fits best?
Viognier is full-bodied and low in acidity, with apricot, peach and blossom: the perfumed white of the Rhône.
A typical Italian Pinot Grigio is…
Light and crisp, with pear and lemon
Rich and oaky, with butter and vanilla
Sweet and perfumed, with lychee and rose
Deep golden and nutty, like a sherry
The grapes are picked early for freshness: a light, delicate, easy white, which is why it sells so well by the glass.
Compared with an Italian Pinot Grigio, an Alsace Pinot Gris is usually…
Richer and fuller, often a touch sweet
Lighter and sharper, with less flavour
Red, from long contact with the skins
Sparkling, made in a pressure tank
Same grape, two styles: Italy picks early for a light, crisp wine, Alsace picks ripe for a rich, spicy, honeyed one.
What colour are the skins of ripe Pinot Gris (Pinot Grigio) grapes?
“Gris” and “grigio” mean grey. The pinkish skins explain the coppery tint of some Pinot Grigio.
Which grape family gives wines that smell of fresh grapes and orange blossom?
Muscat is the rare grape whose wine smells of the grape itself. It is made dry, sweet and sparkling.
Which Loire grape gives dry, sweet and sparkling whites with apple, quince and honey notes?
Chenin Blanc’s high acidity suits every style, from bone-dry to lusciously sweet, and lets the best wines age for decades.
Grüner Veltliner is famous for which spicy note beside its citrus and green apple?
A dry, zesty white: “citrus, green apple and a pinch of white pepper” is all you need to say at the table.
Grüner Veltliner is the signature white grape of which country?
It is Austria’s most planted grape, at its best along the Danube in the Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal.
Albariño, the white grape of Galicia in Spain, is typically…
Crisp and aromatic, with peach and citrus
Rich and buttery, with vanilla from oak
Sweet and low in acid, with rose notes
Albariño from Rías Baixas is a seaside white: high acidity, stone fruit and often a salty note.
What does “Gewürz” in Gewürztraminer mean in German?
The name means “spiced Traminer”: a wine perfumed with lychee, rose and sweet spice.
Besides its perfume, a typical Gewürztraminer is…
The grapes ripen to high sugar: a rich, oily wine, often off-dry and high in alcohol, with soft acidity.
Most Sauvignon Blanc is at its best…
After ten years or more in bottle
After several years in new oak
After two hours in a decanter
Its green, zesty aromas fade with time, so most bottles are meant to be drunk within a few years.
Compared with Sancerre, a Sauvignon Blanc from Marlborough, New Zealand, is usually…
Softer and buttery from new oak
Loire Sauvignon is restrained and mineral; New Zealand’s is loud: passion fruit, gooseberry, cut grass.
The “Sauvignon” in Sauvignon Blanc comes from the French word for…
From “sauvage”, wild: the vine once grew like a wild plant in western France.
Pedro Ximénez (PX) is a grape best known for…
Tannic dry red for long ageing
PX grapes are dried in the sun, giving a syrupy wine of raisin, fig and coffee: a dessert in a glass.
A classic Riesling from the Mosel in Germany is…
Light, low in alcohol, with racy acidity
Full-bodied, high in alcohol and oaky
Soft, buttery and low in acidity
Mosel Riesling is delicate and often off-dry, with green apple, lime and a slate note, at well under 12% alcohol.
Which of these is a white grape?
Viognier is a perfumed white from the Rhône. Malbec, Gamay and Barbera are all black grapes for red wine.
Which aromas are typical of Cabernet Sauvignon?
Sour cherry, tea and dried herbs
Blackcurrant (cassis) is the calling card of Cabernet Sauvignon; cedar and cigar box come with oak and age.
How would you describe a typical Cabernet Sauvignon to a guest?
Dark and full-bodied, with firm tannins
Pale and light, with silky tannins
Light and juicy, best lightly chilled
Soft and sweetish, with low acidity
Small, thick-skinned berries give deep colour, firm tannin and fresh acidity: a red built to age.
Which red grape often shows a green bell pepper note when it is not fully ripe?
The leafy note comes from compounds called pyrazines, which fade as the grapes ripen in the sun.
DNA testing showed that the two parents of Cabernet Sauvignon are…
One red grape and one white grape
A red grape and a wild forest vine
Two white grapes from the Loire
Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc crossed by chance in south-west France; the proof came in the 1990s.
A young Pinot Noir typically smells of…
Pinot Noir is about red fruit and perfume, not power: silky tannins and fresh acidity.
With age, a fine Pinot Noir develops aromas of…
Old Burgundy moves from fresh cherry to earthy, savoury notes the French call “sous-bois”, undergrowth.
Why is Pinot Noir usually pale and low in tannin?
It is blended with white grapes
It is fermented without its skins
It is picked before it colours
Colour and tannin come from the skins, and Pinot Noir has less of both than thick-skinned Cabernet or Syrah.
Which grape is nicknamed the “heartbreak grape” because it is so hard to grow well?
Thin-skinned and fussy about climate, Pinot Noir suffers easily from frost, rot and heat.
Compared with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot is usually…
Softer and rounder, with plummy fruit
Pale and light, almost like a rosé
Merlot ripens earlier and has softer tannins: plum, black cherry, chocolate. It is the gentle half of a Bordeaux blend.
Which spice note is the signature of Syrah?
Syrah gives dark, full reds of blackberry, black pepper and violet, with smoked meat and olive in the Rhône.
Which of these red grapes gives the darkest, most deeply coloured wine?
Syrah has thick, dark skins: its wine is almost opaque, purple-black when young.
Which of these red grapes gives the lightest wine, with the least tannin?
Gamay is juicy and light: cherry, raspberry, hardly any tannin. It is one of the few reds that are lovely lightly chilled.
Deep purple and full, with ripe plum
Pale and light, with strawberry notes
Brick-orange, with tar and fierce tannin
Malbec is inky and velvety: ripe plum, blackberry and violet, with soft, ripe tannins.
Carmenère was rediscovered in 1994, growing unnoticed among vines of which grape?
In Chile it had been sold for decades as Merlot. Expect dark fruit with a herbal, green pepper edge.
Sangiovese is the classic red grape of which country?
It is Italy’s most planted red grape, at its best on the hills of Tuscany.
Sour cherry and herbs, with high acidity
Lychee and rose, with some sweetness
A savoury red: sour cherry, tomato leaf and tea, with firm tannins and mouth-watering acidity.
“Tar and roses” is the classic description of which grape?
Nebbiolo smells of rose, tar, cherry and truffle: one of the most recognisable noses in red wine.
Which grape gives pale wines that are nonetheless very high in tannin and acidity?
The colour fools the eye: the wine looks light and brick-tinged, then grips the mouth. It needs time or a decanter.
The name Nebbiolo is linked to “nebbia”, the Italian word for…
The grape ripens late, in October, when autumn fog fills the hills of Piedmont.
Grenache typically gives reds that are…
High in alcohol, with ripe strawberry
Low in alcohol, pale and very sharp
Grenache loves heat: generous, warm, spicy reds with soft tannins and low acidity. It also makes many rosés.
Barbera, the everyday red of Piedmont, combines deep colour with…
Juicy, cherry-fruited and mouth-watering, with soft tannins: a very food-friendly red.
Dolcetto means “little sweet one”. What is the wine actually like?
The name refers to the sweet-tasting grapes. The wine is dry, with black cherry and a bitter almond finish, to drink young.
Tempranillo takes its name from the Spanish for “early”. Why?
It ripens earlier than most red grapes
Its wine must be drunk in the first year
It is always picked before sunrise
It was the first vine planted in Spain
“Temprano” means early: it ripens weeks before Garnacha, the grape it is most often blended with.
“White Zinfandel” from California is in fact…
An off-dry rosé from a black grape
A dry white from a white grape
Zinfandel is a black grape. Its “white” version is a pink, slightly sweet wine, also called blush.
A red Zinfandel from California is typically…
Ripe and jammy, with high alcohol
Pale and delicate, with low alcohol
Lean and green, with sharp tannins
Blackberry jam, raisin and sweet spice, with plenty of alcohol: a big, warm red.
Compared with Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc is usually…
Lighter, with raspberry and leafy notes
Darker, heavier and much more tannic
Cabernet Franc is the lighter, perfumed Cabernet: raspberry, violet, pencil shavings and a leafy green note.
Lambrusco, both a grape and a wine from northern Italy, is typically…
A still, tannic red for ageing
Frizzante, fruity and fresh, made dry or sweet: the classic partner of the cured meats of Emilia.
Which of these is a black grape, used for red wine?
Tempranillo is Spain’s great red grape. Albariño and Verdejo are Spanish whites, Sémillon a white from Bordeaux.
Chablis is made entirely from which grape?
Chablis is Chardonnay at its leanest, with little or no oak. Guests who “don’t like Chardonnay” often love it.
Which grape is Chianti based on?
Every Chianti is built on Sangiovese: sour cherry, herbs, firm tannins and lively acidity.
Which three grapes are the main ones of Champagne?
Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Sémillon
One white grape and two black ones. Most Champagne is a blend of all three.
A white wine from black grapes only
A rosé wine from black grapes only
A white wine from Chardonnay only
A red sparkling wine from Pinot Noir
Pinot Noir and Meunier have clear juice: pressed quickly, they give a white wine with more body and red-fruit depth.
Meunier, the third grape of Champagne, is…
A black grape related to Pinot Noir
A white grape related to Chardonnay
A pink grape used only for rosé
A white grape related to Riesling
Meunier means “miller”: its leaves look dusted with flour. It adds soft, fruity roundness to a blend.
In a Champagne blend, what does Pinot Noir mainly bring?
The bubbles and the creamy foam
Chardonnay gives finesse and citrus, Pinot Noir body and backbone, Meunier soft, early-drinking fruit.
Shiraz is another name for which grape?
Australia says Shiraz, France says Syrah: the same dark, peppery grape, often riper and jammier under the Shiraz name.
Which grape leads the blend of Amarone and Valpolicella?
Corvina gives the sour cherry note; Rondinella is its usual partner. For Amarone the grapes are dried first.
Pouilly-Fumé, from the Loire, is made from which grape?
It faces Sancerre across the river and shares its grape. “Fumé” hints at the smoky, flinty note of the wine.
Pouilly-Fuissé, from southern Burgundy, is made from which grape?
A round, ripe white from the Mâconnais. Do not confuse it with Pouilly-Fumé from the Loire, a different grape altogether.
Which grape is the backbone of Sauternes, the sweet wine of Bordeaux?
Thin-skinned Sémillon takes noble rot easily; Sauvignon Blanc adds freshness to the blend.
Asti, the sweet sparkling wine of Piedmont, is made from which grape?
Asti and Moscato d’Asti are sweet, light and low in alcohol, with fresh grape, peach and blossom.
Soave, the dry white from near Verona, is made mainly from…
Garganega gives a gentle dry white of almond, pear and citrus.
Which grape is the base of almost all dry sherry?
Palomino is neutral by itself: the taste of a fino or an amontillado comes from ageing under flor and in the solera.
The crisp white wines of Rueda, in Spain, are made mainly from…
Verdejo gives an aromatic dry white: citrus, fennel and a pleasantly bitter finish.
What do the letters GSM stand for on a red blend?
The classic southern Rhône trio: Grenache for warmth and fruit, Syrah for colour and spice, Mourvèdre for structure.
Garnacha is the Spanish name of which grape?
As Garnacha it gives warm, ripe reds and rosados in Navarra, Aragón and Priorat.
Primitivo from Puglia is genetically the same grape as…
Both go back to an old Croatian grape. Either way, expect ripe, jammy dark fruit and generous alcohol.
Monastrell, the red grape of south-east Spain, is known in France as…
Dark, meaty and tannic, it loves heat: Jumilla and Yecla in Spain, Bandol in Provence.
“Fumé Blanc” on a Californian label is which grape?
Robert Mondavi coined the name in the 1960s for a dry, often oak-aged style of the grape.
Which trio of grapes is the classic blend of Cava?
Cava is made by the traditional method, like Champagne, but from Catalonia’s own white grapes.
Muscadet, the dry white of the Loire, is made from which grape?
Despite the name it has nothing to do with Muscat: Muscadet is light, dry and salty, the oyster wine of the Loire.
Touriga Nacional is the most prized grape of which wine?
Port is always a blend of local grapes; Touriga Nacional gives it deep colour, firm tannin and a violet perfume.
Cahors, the “black wine” of south-west France, is made mainly from…
Malbec, locally called Côt, was grown here long before Argentina made it famous: dark, firm, plummy wines.
Madiran, the dark red of south-west France, is based on which grape?
Tannat is one of the most tannic grapes there is: dark, powerful reds that need age. It is also Uruguay’s flagship.
Besides Chardonnay, which white grape is traditional in Burgundy?
Aligoté is Burgundy’s second white: light, sharp and lemony. With crème de cassis it makes the original Kir.
Is made almost entirely from one grape
Is made without any added sulphites
Chardonnay or Merlot on the label means a varietal wine; a wine of several grapes is a blend.
A typical Mavrud is a red wine that is…
Pale, light and low in tannins
Light, with a strong Muscat scent
Mavrud has small berries with thick skins, so the wine is deep in colour, firm and well suited to ageing in oak.
The name Mavrud is linked to the Greek word “mavro”. What does it mean?
“Mavro” is Greek for black, a nod to the grape’s very dark skins. The same word is found in Xinomavro and Mavrodaphne.
Which aromas are typical of Mavrud?
Ripe dark fruit with herbs and spice, and leather notes with age. A wine for lamb, game and mature cheese.
A guest wants a light, fresh Bulgarian red. Which grape fits best?
Gamza has thin skins: pale colour, soft tannins and lively freshness. It is good served slightly cool.
Gamza is best known for the aroma of which fruit?
Young Gamza smells of raspberry and sour cherry, sometimes with a peppery touch: an easy match for charcuterie and poultry.
In which part of Bulgaria is Gamza the traditional red grape?
In the north, on the Danubian Plain
In the south-west, in the Struma Valley
In the centre, in the Rose Valley
Gamza is at home around Vidin, Novo Selo, Suhindol and Pleven. In Hungary the same grape is called Kadarka.
Which Bulgarian red grape gives pale, soft wines meant to be drunk young?
Pamid is thin-skinned, with little colour and low acidity: a simple, easy everyday red, best in its first year or two.
Which of these Bulgarian red grapes is an ancient variety, not a 20th-century cross?
Pamid is one of the oldest grapes of these lands. Rubin, Ruen and Bouquet were all bred by Bulgarian scientists in the last century.
With age, wines from Shiroka Melnishka Loza are known for which aroma?
Aged Melnik moves from cherry and herbs towards tobacco and leather. Firm tannins and freshness let it keep for years.
Shiroka Melnishka Loza is known for ripening…
Very early, at the start of August
It needs the long, hot autumn of the Struma Valley to ripen fully, which is why it is grown almost nowhere else.
In the name Shiroka Melnishka Loza, what does “shiroka” (broad) describe?
The wide valley it grows in
The wide spacing of the rows
The full name means “broad-leaved vine of Melnik”. On labels it is often shortened to Melnik.
Melnik 55 was bred from Shiroka Melnishka Loza mainly so that it would…
It is also called Early Melnik (Ranna Melnishka Loza): it ripens well before its parent and gives softer, fruitier reds.
Ruen is a Bulgarian cross of Shiroka Melnishka Loza with which grape?
Ruen keeps Melnik’s spice and adds the dark colour and structure of Cabernet. It is grown mainly in the Struma Valley.
The Bulgarian red grape Bouquet is a cross of Mavrud with…
Bouquet was bred in Bulgaria in the 1950s. Mavrud crossed with Merlot gave another local grape, Evmolpia.
In which city was the Rubin grape created, at the Institute of Viticulture and Enology?
The Pleven institute has bred many Bulgarian grapes. Rubin, its cross of Nebbiolo and Syrah, dates from the 1940s.
Which of these Bulgarian grapes is white?
Dimyat is an old white grape that gives light, fresh wines to drink young. Pamid, Gamza and Mavrud are red.
Which of these Bulgarian grapes gives red wine?
Melnik 55 is a red grape from the Struma Valley. Keratsuda, Gergana and Tamyanka are all white.
Dimyat is the traditional white grape of which Bulgarian region?
Dimyat is at home around Varna, Pomorie and Burgas: light whites with a soft, fruity nose, best in their first years.
In Serbia and North Macedonia, Dimyat is grown under which name?
Smederevka is named after the Serbian town of Smederevo, on the Danube. Same grape, same light, fresh white wine.
Which aromatic grape is traditional around Karlovo and Sungurlare, south of the Balkan range?
Misket Cherven is also sold as Karlovski or Sungurlarski Misket: a dry white with a floral, lightly spicy nose.
Which town in north-west Bulgaria gives its name to a local aromatic Misket grape?
Vrachanski Misket gives perfumed whites with Muscat, flower and spice notes, made dry or a little sweeter.
What does a typical dry Tamyanka smell of?
Tamyanka is a Muscat: very perfumed, with rose, orange blossom and a hint of incense, which gave the grape its name.
Gergana is a Bulgarian cross of Muscat Ottonel with which local white grape?
Gergana is grown mainly near the Black Sea and joins Dimyat’s freshness to a gentle Muscat scent.
Keratsuda is a rare local white grape of which Bulgarian region?
Keratsuda grows almost only in the far south-west, around Kresna and Sandanski. Few wineries bottle it on its own.
Rkatsiteli, a white grape widely planted in Bulgaria, comes originally from…
Rkatsiteli is an ancient Georgian grape with high acidity. At home it is often fermented on its skins in qvevri.
Romania’s Tămâioasă Românească is the same grape as which Bulgarian favourite?
Both are Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, and both names come from the word for incense. In Serbia it is Tamjanika.
Which of these red grapes is native to Bulgaria?
Mavrud is Bulgarian. Saperavi is Georgian, Xinomavro is Greek and Vranec comes from the western Balkans.
Which of these white grapes is a local Bulgarian variety?
Misket Cherven is an old Bulgarian grape with pink skins and a floral white wine. The other three were brought in from abroad.
In Bulgarian grape names, what does the word “Misket” point to?
Misket is the Bulgarian word for Muscat. Misket Cherven and Vrachanski Misket are both scented, flowery whites.
How many protected geographical indications (PGI) for wine does Bulgaria have?
Danubian Plain in the north and Thracian Lowlands in the south. Names like Melnik or Sakar are narrower appellations inside them.
It takes in the country south of the Balkan Mountains, from the Struma Valley to the southern Black Sea coast.
Bulgaria’s northern wine PGI is named after which river?
PGI Danubian Plain stretches from the Danube to the Balkan Mountains: Vidin, Pleven, Svishtov, Ruse and on to the east.
Which mountain range separates Bulgaria’s northern wine country from the southern?
North of the range lies the Danubian Plain, south of it the Thracian Lowlands: the two halves of Bulgarian wine.
Which Bulgarian wine region lies in the far south-west, towards Greece and North Macedonia?
Warm air comes up the Struma from the Aegean, so this is the most Mediterranean corner of the country. Melnik is its wine town.
In which part of Bulgaria is Sakar, known for its red wines?
In the south-west, near North Macedonia
Sakar is a low mountain around Harmanli and Lyubimets. Its hot, dry summers ripen Merlot, Cabernet and Syrah fully.
The wine town of Melnik lies at the foot of which mountain?
Melnik sits on the south-western slopes of Pirin. Its old cellars are dug straight into the soft rock.
The Bulgarian Black Sea region is best known for which wines?
The sea makes autumn long and mild, so white grapes ripen slowly and keep their aromas: Dimyat, Riesling, Chardonnay, Traminer.
Compared with the south, the climate of the Danubian Plain is…
Cool and rainy all summer long
Nothing shelters the north from cold winds, so winters are harsher. Whites and lighter reds like Gamza do well here.
Besides wine, what is the town of Melnik famous for?
The Melnik pyramids are tall eroded sandstone cliffs all around the town, a classic stop on a wine trip to the south-west.
Which wine region lies between the Balkan Mountains and Sredna Gora?
The sheltered Sub-Balkan valleys are known for aromatic whites, above all Misket Cherven, and for rose oil.
The Thracian Lowlands are best known for which style of wine?
Warm summers and shelter from northern winds ripen Mavrud, Rubin, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon fully.
In which month is Trifon Zarezan celebrated?
The church keeps it on 1 February and many people on 14 February, the old-calendar date: the start of the vineyard year.
What do vine growers traditionally do in the vineyard on Trifon Zarezan?
A few shoots are cut and the vine is watered with wine, for a rich harvest. Then the feast begins.
On Trifon Zarezan, the village traditionally chooses a…
The “king” is crowned with a wreath of vine shoots and carried through the village, to bring a fruitful year.
Which god of wine did the ancient Thracians worship?
Ancient writers placed a sanctuary of Dionysus in the Thracian mountains. Wine was part of Thracian rites and feasts.
A rhyton, found in many Thracian treasures, is…
A clay jar for storing grain
A bronze knife for pruning vines
A stone press for crushing grapes
The gold Panagyurishte treasure is a whole Thracian wine set, with rhyta that end in the heads of animals.
In Homer’s Iliad, ships bring wine to the Greek camp at Troy from…
Homer already knew Thracian wine. In the Odyssey, a strong wine from Thrace is what gets the Cyclops drunk.
According to legend, which Bulgarian ruler ordered the country’s vineyards uprooted?
The legend goes on: a young man called Mavrud, raised on hidden wine, killed a lion, and the khan let the vines return.
Unlike the ancient Greeks, the Thracians were known for drinking their wine…
Mixed with a lot of water
Greeks mixed their wine with water and thought neat wine barbaric. Ancient authors say the Thracians drank it pure.
Fortified wine aged in the sun
Wormwood and other herbs are steeped in the wine, which turns pleasantly bitter. It is served well chilled.
Which affordable wine made Bulgaria known in Western Europe in the 1980s?
Bulgarian Cabernet was a supermarket favourite in Britain. The focus on local grapes like Mavrud came later.
Saperavi is the best-known red grape of which country?
Saperavi gives inky, sharp, long-lived reds, dry or semi-sweet. Guests from the former Soviet countries often know it well.
What is unusual about the Saperavi grape?
Its flesh and juice are red
Its skin stays green when ripe
Its grapes ripen in early summer
Most red grapes have clear juice and colour only in the skin. Saperavi means “dye”, hence its almost black wines.
A large clay jar buried in the ground
A small oak barrel for sweet wine
A stone trough for treading grapes
The grapes ferment and the wine rests in the qvevri for months, often with skins and stalks. The earth keeps it cool.
Georgian whites fermented on their skins in qvevri are known as…
Months on the skins give a deep amber colour, tea-like tannins and notes of dried apricot and nuts. Elsewhere it is called orange wine.
Which region in the east of Georgia makes most of the country’s wine?
Kakheti is the home of Saperavi and Rkatsiteli and of famous wine villages such as Tsinandali and Mukuzani.
At a Georgian feast, who is the “tamada”?
At a supra, the Georgian feast, the tamada proposes every toast in turn, and nobody drinks before he has spoken.
Kindzmarauli, a Georgian wine that guests often ask for, is…
A dry amber wine from qvevri
It comes from Kakheti and keeps some natural grape sugar. For a dry Saperavi, the classic name is Mukuzani.
Historic Thrace is shared today by Bulgaria, Greece and which other country?
Wine is made in all three parts. Turkish Thrace, just across the border, is one of Turkey’s main wine areas.
Öküzgözü and Boğazkere are native red grapes of which country?
Both come from eastern Anatolia and are often blended: Öküzgözü for fruit and freshness, Boğazkere for tannin.
Turkey grows a huge amount of grapes. What are most of them used for?
Only a small share becomes wine, yet the country has many native grapes, such as Öküzgözü, Narince and Emir.
The Turkish grape name Öküzgözü means…
The berries are big, round and dark, like the eye of an ox. Its usual partner Boğazkere means “throat burner”.
The Greek white grape Assyrtiko comes originally from which island?
From Santorini it has spread all over Greece, loved for its bone-dry, salty, citrus style.
What sets Assyrtiko apart from most white grapes of hot climates?
It has a strong Muscat aroma
Even fully ripe it stays sharp and mineral, which is why it goes so well with grilled fish and seafood.
How are vines traditionally trained on Santorini?
As low baskets on the ground
The basket, called “kouloura”, is woven from the vine’s own canes and shields the grapes from fierce wind and burning sun.
The vineyards of Santorini grow on which kind of soil?
The island is the rim of a volcano. Phylloxera cannot live in this soil, so many vines are very old and ungrafted.
A sweet wine from sun-dried grapes
A dry white flavoured with pine resin
A dry red aged in clay jars
Mostly Assyrtiko, dried in the sun and then aged for years in barrel: amber, with raisin, coffee and lively acidity.
Xinomavro is the grape of which Greek appellation?
Naoussa, in Greek Macedonia, is pure Xinomavro: pale, tannic and sharp when young, and very long-lived.
For its high tannins and acidity, Xinomavro is most often compared to…
Like Barolo, a good Xinomavro is pale but powerful, with tomato, olive and dried rose notes, and it needs time.
What does the Greek grape name Xinomavro mean?
“Xino” is sour and “mavro” is black: the name warns of the grape’s sharp acidity and dark skins.
Agiorgitiko is the red grape of which Greek region?
Nemea is in the Peloponnese. Its Agiorgitiko, “St George’s grape”, gives soft reds with plum and sweet spice.
What gives the Greek wine Retsina its special taste?
A little Aleppo pine resin is added during fermentation, a habit from the days when amphorae were sealed with resin.
Which white grape is the traditional base of Retsina?
Savatiano is the main grape of Attica, around Athens, and copes well with heat and drought. Roditis is often blended in.
The Greek island of Samos is famous for sweet wines made from…
Samos grows Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains on steep terraces. It is the same grape as Bulgarian Tamyanka.
A dry white with pine resin
A light dry red, drunk young
Dark and port-like, with raisin, chocolate and caramel notes. Serve it lightly chilled with dessert or cheese.
Moschofilero, from Mantinia in the Peloponnese, gives wines that are…
The grape is pink-skinned, so the wine can show a faint blush. Expect rose petal, citrus and crisp freshness.
Vranec is the leading red grape of which neighbour of Bulgaria?
Vranec is North Macedonia’s signature red. In Montenegro, where it is just as important, the name is written Vranac.
What does the grape name Vranec mean?
“Vran” is an old Slavic word for black, and a vranec is a black horse: strong and spirited, like the wine.
A pale, light red served chilled
Deep colour, ripe blackberry and plum, firm tannins and often high alcohol: a wine for grilled meat.
Most of North Macedonia’s vineyards lie in the valley of which river?
The Vardar valley, with the Tikveš district at its heart, is hot and dry: ideal for ripe reds like Vranec.
Prokupac is a native red grape of which country?
Prokupac gives juicy, medium-bodied reds with cherry and spice, and is Serbia’s best-known native red.
Bermet, an aromatised sweet wine, is a speciality of which region?
Bermet is made around Sremski Karlovci from wine steeped with herbs and spices, a little like a vermouth.
Which of these Romanian grapes gives red wine?
“Neagră” means black. Fetească Neagră gives dark reds with plum and spice, while Albă and Regală are white grapes.
The Romanian grape name Fetească comes from a word meaning…
“Fată” is a girl in Romanian, so Fetească is “the maiden’s grape”. Three different grapes share the name.
What is Cotnari, in north-eastern Romania, historically famous for?
Grasă de Cotnari, often touched by noble rot, gives golden sweet wines that were long compared with Tokaji.
Dealu Mare, a region known for its red wines, lies in which country?
Dealu Mare, “the big hill”, lies on the Carpathian foothills north of Bucharest. Fetească Neagră does very well here.
Tokaj, famous for its sweet wines, is a wine region of which country?
Tokaj lies in north-eastern Hungary, where two rivers meet and autumn mists bring noble rot to the grapes.
Which grape is the backbone of Tokaj wines?
Furmint takes noble rot easily and keeps its freshness for decades. Hárslevelű and a little Muscat complete the blend.
“Aszú” are the shrivelled berries, picked one by one and soaked in base wine. Hence honey, apricot and sharp acidity.
On a bottle of Tokaji Aszú, what does the number of “puttonyos” show?
How many years it has aged
How strong it is in alcohol
How many grapes are in the blend
A puttony was the basket of aszú berries added to each barrel: the more baskets, the sweeter the wine.
It is a blend built on Kékfrankos, from Eger in northern Hungary. Legend ties the name to the siege of Eger castle in 1552.
High in acidity, firm and mineral
Soft, low in acidity and buttery
Expect apple, pear and quince, often a smoky note from Tokaj’s volcanic soils. It handles oak and rich fish dishes well.
The free-run juice of aszú berries
Juice boiled down to a syrup
The juice that drips from piled aszú berries under their own weight is so sweet it barely ferments: just a few degrees of alcohol.
Tokaj’s noble rot depends on autumn mists rising from which two rivers?
Damp, misty mornings start the noble rot and sunny afternoons dry the berries. The same pattern makes Sauternes in France.
Which of these grapes from Bulgaria’s neighbours is white?
Assyrtiko is Greece’s great white grape. Vranec, Xinomavro and Prokupac all give red wine.
Sancerre is a white wine from which French region?
Sancerre sits at the eastern end of the Loire and is the benchmark for crisp, mineral whites.
Which grape is white Sancerre made from?
Sancerre and its neighbour Pouilly-Fumé are the classic French homes of Sauvignon Blanc.
Médoc, Saint-Émilion and Pomerol are parts of which wine region?
Médoc is on the Left Bank of Bordeaux, Saint-Émilion and Pomerol on the Right Bank.
Chablis belongs to which French wine region?
Chablis lies far north of the rest of Burgundy, which is why its wines are so lean and fresh.
The great red wines of Burgundy are made from which grape?
Red Burgundy is Pinot Noir on its own, never a blend: the name of the village tells you the style.
Real Champagne can come only from which country?
Only wine from the Champagne region in north-east France may carry the name. Everything else is sparkling wine.
Which French region is famous above all for pale, dry rosé?
Most of the wine made in Provence is rosé, and its pale, dry style is copied all over the world.
Alsace, known for Riesling and Gewürztraminer, is a region of…
Alsace lies on the German border and uses German grapes and tall bottles, but it is French.
Sauternes, from Bordeaux, is famous as a…
Sauternes is golden and honeyed, made from grapes shrivelled by noble rot. A classic with dessert or blue cheese.
A guest orders Chablis. What style should they expect?
Chablis is always a dry white: lean, mineral, with high acidity and little or no oak flavour.
Bordeaux is best known for which kind of wine?
Around nine bottles in ten from Bordeaux are red, almost always a blend of several grapes.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape belongs to which French wine region?
It is the most famous name of the southern Rhône: warm, full-bodied reds named after the popes of Avignon.
Beaujolais, known for light, fruity reds, is made from which grape?
Gamay gives juicy reds with soft tannins, which is why Beaujolais is often served lightly chilled.
Which grape leads the blends of Saint-Émilion and Pomerol?
The clay soils of Bordeaux’s Right Bank suit Merlot, so the wines are rounder and softer than in the Médoc.
The Médoc, on Bordeaux’s Left Bank, is best known for blends led by…
The gravel soils of the Médoc ripen Cabernet Sauvignon, giving firm, tannic wines built to age.
Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie, in the northern Rhône, are red wines from…
Syrah is the only red grape of the northern Rhône. Grenache takes over further south.
Which grape leads most red Châteauneuf-du-Pape?
The appellation allows many grapes, but Grenache is the backbone, usually with Syrah and Mourvèdre.
Vouvray, in the Loire Valley, is made from which grape?
Vouvray can be dry, sweet or sparkling, but it is always Chenin Blanc. Ask which style the bottle is.
Muscadet is a dry white wine from which French region?
Muscadet comes from the mouth of the Loire, near the Atlantic. Despite the name it has nothing to do with Muscat.
Gevrey-Chambertin and Meursault are villages of which wine region?
In Burgundy the village is the name on the label: Gevrey-Chambertin for reds, Meursault for whites.
Morgon, Fleurie and Moulin-à-Vent are crus of…
The ten crus are the best villages of Beaujolais. Their labels often show only the village name.
Chianti comes from which Italian region?
Chianti is made in the hills between Florence and Siena, mainly from Sangiovese.
Barolo comes from which Italian region?
Barolo comes from the Langhe hills in north-west Italy and is often called “the king of wines”.
Barolo and Barbaresco are both made from which grape?
Nebbiolo looks pale but brings firm tannins and high acidity, so these wines need time and food.
Prosecco is a sparkling wine from which country?
Prosecco comes from north-east Italy, around Veneto, and is usually lighter and fruitier than Champagne.
Brunello di Montalcino is made entirely from which grape?
Brunello is the local name of the grape in Montalcino, Tuscany. No other variety is allowed in the wine.
Which is the highest classification for Italian wine?
The G stands for “garantita”, guaranteed: these bottles carry a numbered seal on the neck.
“Classico” on an Italian label, as in Chianti Classico, means the wine…
Comes from the historic core zone
Was aged longer in oak barrels
Is made by the traditional method
Classico marks the original, usually hillier core of a region, as it was before the zone was enlarged.
“Riserva” on an Italian label means the wine…
Is sweeter than the basic wine
A Riserva spends extra time in the cellar, so expect a more developed wine than the basic bottling.
The name Amarone on a label promises…
Amarone is made in Valpolicella from grapes dried for months, which gives a rich wine, high in alcohol.
Valpolicella and Soave come from which Italian region?
Both are grown around Verona: Valpolicella is a red wine, Soave a dry white.
Sweet, lightly sparkling, low in alcohol
Dry, still and high in alcohol
Dry, fully sparkling, high in alcohol
Sweet, still and fortified with spirit
Moscato d’Asti from Piedmont has only about 5% alcohol and smells of fresh grapes: easy with fruit desserts.
“Rosso” on an Italian label means the wine is…
Rosso is red, rosato is rosé and bianco is white.
“Spumante” on an Italian label means the wine is…
Spumante is fully sparkling. “Frizzante” means only lightly sparkling.
Franciacorta, a traditional-method sparkling wine, comes from which Italian region?
Franciacorta is made like Champagne, with the second fermentation in the bottle, mostly from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
Which grape is Prosecco made from?
The grape itself used to be called Prosecco. It was renamed Glera in 2009 so that the name protects the region.
Marsala is a fortified wine from which Italian region?
Marsala is named after a port town in western Sicily. It comes dry or sweet and is also famous in the kitchen.
Etna Rosso, the red wine of Sicily’s volcano, is based on which grape?
Nerello Mascalese gives pale, elegant reds on Etna’s high lava soils, often compared to Pinot Noir.
Rioja is a wine region of which country?
Rioja lies along the river Ebro in the north of Spain and is the country’s best-known red wine.
The main red grape of Rioja is…
Tempranillo is the backbone of Rioja, often blended with a little Garnacha.
On a Rioja label, which term promises the longest ageing?
The ladder goes Joven, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva: each step means more time in oak and in bottle.
“Crianza” on a Spanish red tells you the wine was…
Aged in oak, then in bottle
Crianza is the first rung of oak-aged Spanish wine: younger and fruitier than a Reserva.
Which of these sparkling wines is Spanish?
Cava is made by the traditional method, like Champagne, mostly in Catalonia near Barcelona.
Sherry comes from around the town of Jerez, in which part of Spain?
The word “sherry” is the English form of Jerez, a town in the hot far south of Spain.
Fino and Manzanilla are styles of…
Both are pale and bone-dry, the lightest of their family, and are served well chilled as an aperitif.
Rías Baixas, in Galicia, is known for which white grape?
Albariño from Spain’s rainy Atlantic corner is crisp and slightly salty, a natural match for seafood.
Priorat, known for powerful reds from old vines, is in which Spanish region?
Priorat lies in the hills inland from Tarragona: steep slate slopes with old Garnacha and Cariñena vines.
Port is a fortified wine from which country?
Port takes its name from the city of Porto, from where the wine has been shipped for centuries.
The grapes for Port grow in which river valley?
The steep terraces of the Douro Valley in northern Portugal also make excellent dry red wines.
Ruby and Tawny are styles of…
Ruby is young, dark and fruity. Tawny is aged in wood and turns amber and nutty.
Madeira is a fortified wine from…
A Portuguese island in the Atlantic
A Spanish island in the Mediterranean
A river valley in northern Portugal
A coastal town in southern Italy
Madeira is deliberately heated as it ages, which is why an open bottle keeps for months.
“Tinto” on a Spanish or Portuguese label means the wine is…
Tinto is red, blanco or branco is white, and rosado is rosé.
Quinta is Portuguese for a farm or estate, much like château in Bordeaux: Quinta do Noval, Quinta do Crasto.
The Mosel is a famous wine region of which country?
The steep slate slopes above the river Mosel give light, delicate whites, often low in alcohol.
Which grape is the star of Germany’s Mosel and Rheingau?
German Riesling runs from bone-dry to very sweet, so always check the label for the style.
“Trocken” on a German or Austrian label means the wine is…
Trocken is dry and halbtrocken is off-dry. Without either word, a German Riesling often has some sweetness.
Which German Prädikat is the lightest, from the least ripe grapes?
The ladder rises with ripeness: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese.
“Spätlese” on a German label literally means…
Spätlese grapes are picked later and riper than Kabinett. The wine may be sweet or, if marked trocken, dry.
Despite “trocken” in its name, a Trockenbeerenauslese is…
Here “trocken” describes the berries, dried on the vine by noble rot. It is among the sweetest wines in the world.
“Sekt” on a German or Austrian label means…
Sekt is the German word for sparkling wine. It sounds like the French “sec”, but says nothing about sweetness.
The Wachau is a famous wine region of which country?
The Wachau is a steep stretch of the Danube west of Vienna, known for dry Riesling and Grüner Veltliner.
“Spätburgunder” on a German label is which grape?
Burgunder means “from Burgundy”: Spätburgunder is Pinot Noir, Grauburgunder is Pinot Gris.
Napa Valley is in which US state?
Napa, north of San Francisco, is America’s most famous wine region, known above all for Cabernet Sauvignon.
Mendoza is the main wine region of which country?
Mendoza lies at the foot of the Andes, with some of the highest vineyards in the world.
Which red grape is Argentina’s flagship?
Malbec came from south-west France but found its fame in Argentina: dark, plummy and smooth.
Marlborough, famous for Sauvignon Blanc, is in which country?
Marlborough, at the top of the South Island, made New Zealand’s name with its punchy, aromatic Sauvignon Blanc.
The Barossa Valley is a wine region of which country?
The Barossa, near Adelaide, still farms some of the oldest vines in the world, planted in the 1840s.
The Barossa Valley is best known for which grape?
Shiraz is the Australian name for Syrah. Barossa versions are rich, ripe and full-bodied.
Carmenère is the signature red grape of which country?
Carmenère came from Bordeaux and was long mistaken for Merlot in Chile, until it was identified in 1994.
Pinotage is the signature red grape of which country?
Pinotage was bred in South Africa in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsault.
Oregon’s Willamette Valley is best known for which grape?
Oregon is cooler and wetter than California, which suits Pinot Noir: its wines are often compared to Burgundy.
AVA is the appellation system of which country?
An AVA (American Viticultural Area), such as Napa Valley, defines only where the grapes grow, not which grapes or methods.
Australia’s Hunter Valley is famous for long-lived dry whites from…
Hunter Semillon is light and lemony when young and turns toasty and honeyed with age, without any oak.
Which of these is a wine region of New Zealand?
Central Otago, in the far south, is one of the most southerly wine regions in the world and is known for Pinot Noir.
“Brut” on a Champagne label means the wine is…
Brut is the standard dry style of Champagne and of most sparkling wine: the safe choice for an aperitif.
Which of these sparkling-wine terms means the driest wine?
From dry to sweet: Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut, Extra Dry, Sec, Demi-sec, Doux. Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut.
Demi-sec literally means “half-dry”, but it holds far more sugar than a Brut: a sparkling wine for dessert.
“Vieilles Vignes” on a French label means the wine comes from…
Old vines give fewer but more concentrated grapes. French law sets no minimum age, so it is a promise, not a guarantee.
In Burgundy, which vineyard rank is the highest?
Burgundy’s ladder is regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru. The rank belongs to the vineyard, not to the producer.
What does AOC or AOP on a French label guarantee?
The appellation ties a wine to a defined area and to that area’s rules on grapes and yields.
Fortified wine from the far south
Crémant is made by the traditional method, like Champagne, in regions such as Alsace, Burgundy and the Loire.
“Blanc de Blancs” on a Champagne label means it is made…
In Champagne that almost always means pure Chardonnay. “Blanc de Noirs” is a white wine from black grapes.
What do Alsace labels show that most classic French labels do not?
Alsace bottles say Riesling, Pinot Gris or Gewürztraminer on the front, which makes them easy to explain to a guest.
Condrieu, in the northern Rhône, is a white wine made from…
Condrieu is the original home of Viognier: full-bodied whites that smell of apricot and blossom.
Chinon and Bourgueil, red wines of the Loire, are made from…
The Loire is the home of pure Cabernet Franc: medium-bodied reds with fresh acidity and a leafy note.
In the Wachau, which term marks the ripest, fullest dry whites?
The Wachau has its own ladder: Steinfeder is the lightest, Federspiel the middle, Smaragd the richest, named after a green lizard.
The soil, climate and site of a vineyard
The grape variety a wine is made from
The winemaker’s techniques in the cellar
The year in which the grapes were picked
Terroir is why the same grape tastes different from two vineyards: the place leaves its mark on the wine.
When are wine grapes usually harvested in Europe?
Grapes for sparkling wine come first, late reds last. Ice wine, picked in winter, is the rare exception.
When is the grape harvest in the southern hemisphere, for example in Chile or Australia?
The seasons are reversed, so a southern wine is about half a year older than a European one of the same vintage.
Phylloxera, which destroyed Europe’s vineyards in the 19th century, is…
An insect that feeds on vine roots
A fungus that covers the leaves
A virus that discolours the leaves
A bacterium that sours the grapes
The tiny louse came from North America in the 1860s and killed most European vines within a few decades.
How were European vines saved from phylloxera?
By grafting them onto American rootstocks
By spraying the leaves with sulphur
By spraying them with copper and lime
By pruning the vines much shorter
American vine roots resist the insect, so almost every vine in Europe today is a European variety on an American root.
In which soil can vines grow ungrafted, because phylloxera cannot live in it?
The insect cannot move through loose sand, so a few sandy vineyards still have very old vines on their own roots.
In a vineyard, what is the “yield”?
The amount of grapes harvested per hectare
The sugar level of the grapes at harvest
The number of vines planted per hectare
The age of the vines at harvest
A lower yield usually means riper, more concentrated grapes, so many quality regions set a maximum.
“Old vines” on a label suggest that the vines give…
An old vine has deep roots and a small crop. There is no single legal age, but it usually means several decades.
Removing some unripe bunches in summer
Picking grapes early for sparkling wine
Picking by hand, without any machines
With fewer bunches to feed, the vine puts its energy into the ones that remain: less wine, but more concentrated.
“Veraison” is the moment in summer when the grapes…
Change colour and begin to ripen
Open their flowers and set fruit
Go through the press for the first time
Start to ferment in the tank
Red grapes turn from green to purple, white ones turn golden and translucent, and sugar starts to build.
Which of these comes first in the vine’s year?
The order is budburst in spring, flowering, fruit set, veraison in summer and then the harvest.
Grapes from a cool climate usually give a wine with…
In cool places grapes ripen slowly, keep their acidity and build less sugar, so the wines are lighter and crisper.
As grapes ripen on the vine, what happens inside them?
Choosing the harvest day is a balance: pick too early and the wine is sharp, too late and it is heavy and flat.
Which vine species gives almost all of the world’s wine?
Chardonnay, Merlot and Mavrud are all Vitis vinifera. The American species are used mainly as rootstocks.
Why do growers fear a frost in late spring?
It kills the young buds and shoots
It freezes the roots deep in the soil
It cracks the old wood of the trunk
It kills the yeast on the grape skins
The new shoots carry the year’s crop, so one cold night in April or May can wipe out much of a vintage.
In Europe, which way do the warmest, sunniest vineyard slopes face?
A south-facing slope catches the sun all day, which is why the best sites in cool regions are planted on them.
How long after planting does a vine usually give its first crop for wine?
A young vine first builds roots and wood. Growers call the first real harvest the “third leaf”.
During fermentation, yeast turns the sugar of the grapes into…
The gas escapes from an open tank. Trap it in a closed bottle or tank and you have a sparkling wine.
The yeast ferments nearly all the sugar
It spends a long time in oak barrels
It takes a lot of tannin from the skins
Part of the water in it is removed
Dry means not sweet. Tannin can make the mouth feel dry, but that is texture, not the wine’s level of sweetness.
An oenologist is a specialist in…
The oenologist works in the cellar, the viticulturist in the vineyard and the sommelier in the restaurant.
Fresh grape juice that has not yet fermented
The dead yeast at the bottom of the tank
The skins and seeds left after pressing
The crust of sediment in an old bottle
Must is the juice, often with skins and seeds, that goes into the tank. Once the yeast has done its work, it is wine.
How much alcohol does a typical dry still wine have?
Beer sits around 4–6% and fortified wines such as Port around 20%. Still wine falls in between.
The skins, seeds and stems left after pressing
The dead yeast that settles in the tank
The juice that runs off before pressing
The crystals that form on the cork
Pomace is not wasted: distilled, it becomes grappa in Italy, marc in France and pomace rakia in the Balkans.
Yeasts that live on the grapes and in the cellar
A selected yeast bought from a laboratory
Brewer’s yeast left over from making beer
No yeast at all, only bacteria
It is slower and riskier than adding cultured yeast, but many producers feel it gives a wine more character.
A winemaker chills a tank to stop the fermentation early. The wine will be…
The sugar the yeast did not eat stays in the wine. Many off-dry German Rieslings are made this way.
Adding sugar to the must to raise the alcohol
Adding sugar to sweeten the finished wine
Adding acid to freshen a flat wine
Adding spirit to stop the fermentation
It is used in cool regions when grapes lack sugar. The yeast ferments the added sugar, so the wine does not get sweeter.
Carbonic maceration, typical of Beaujolais, starts with…
Whole, uncrushed bunches in a sealed tank
Crushed grapes in open vats, stirred by hand
Dried grapes pressed after several months
Clear juice fermented cold in new barrels
The tank is filled with CO2 and fermentation begins inside each berry: a light, juicy red with little tannin.
When are the grapes pressed for a typical white wine?
Only the juice ferments. Red wine is the opposite: it ferments with its skins and is pressed afterwards.
Where does a red wine get its colour?
The colour sits in the skins and passes into the juice while they ferment together.
What colour is the juice of most red grapes?
Press red grapes gently, without the skins, and the wine is white. That is how white Champagne is made from Pinot Noir.
Leaving the juice in contact with the skins
Stirring the lees in the barrel
Colour, tannin and aroma pass from the skins into the juice. Hours give a rosé, weeks give a deep red.
A longer time on the skins gives a red wine…
A light, fruity red may spend a few days on its skins; a wine built to age can stay for several weeks.
Why are some wines not suitable for vegans?
They are clarified with egg white
Wine yeast is an animal product
Barrels are sealed with animal fat
Egg white, casein and fish isinglass are used to clear a wine. Vegan wines use clay (bentonite) or are left unfined.
A guest sees a light haze in a wine labelled “unfiltered”. It is…
Fine particles left in on purpose
A sign that the wine is corked
A sign that it is fermenting again
Some producers skip filtering to keep more flavour and texture. The haze is harmless; pour gently if there is sediment.
How does a still rosé usually get its pink colour?
A few hours of contact with red grape skins
Ageing in barrels that once held red wine
Pressing a grape with naturally pink flesh
Filtering a red wine until it turns pale
Rosé is made from red grapes: the juice is run off the skins after a short time, before it takes on much colour.
In which wine is rosé commonly made by adding a little red wine to white?
Champagne is the classic exception: most rosé Champagne is white wine with a small share of local red blended in.
What does the “saignée” method of making rosé involve?
Bleeding off some juice from a tank of red grapes
Pressing whole red bunches straight away
Blending a little red wine into white
Ageing a pale red wine on its lees
Saignée means “bleeding”. The pink juice becomes rosé, and the red wine left in the tank becomes more concentrated.
A white wine fermented on its grape skins
A wine flavoured with orange peel
A blend of red wine and white wine
A white wine left to oxidise in the sun
White grapes are treated like red ones: days or months on the skins give amber colour, tannin and a tea-like grip.
Which aromas does a new oak barrel give to a wine?
If a guest dislikes “woody” wines, offer one aged in steel or old barrels: vanilla and toast come from new oak.
Why are many crisp white wines fermented in stainless steel?
It is neutral and keeps the fruit pure
It adds vanilla and sweet spice
It softens the tannins of the wine
It lets the wine breathe slowly
Steel gives no flavour, lets in no air and is easy to cool, so the wine tastes of the grape and nothing else.
Which barrel gives a wine the strongest oak flavour?
A new barrel has the most flavour to give, and a small one puts more wood in touch with each litre of wine.
Compared with French oak, American oak typically gives more…
American oak is bolder and sweeter, French oak subtler and spicier. Traditional Rioja is the classic American-oak red.
Heating its inside over a fire as it is made
Rinsing it with hot wine before first use
Drying the staves in the sun for years
Burning sulphur inside it to keep it clean
Light, medium or heavy toast changes the flavour: the heavier the toast, the more smoke, coffee and caramel.
Besides flavour, what does an oak barrel give a wine that a steel tank does not?
A slow, gentle contact with oxygen
Wood breathes a little. That trickle of air softens tannins and rounds the wine, which is why reds mature in barrel.
Dead yeast cells that settle after fermentation
Grape skins and seeds left after pressing
Crystals of acid that form in the cold
Grape sugar that the yeast did not eat
Wine left on its fine lees gains a creamier texture. On a label you may see “sur lie”: aged on the lees.
Stirring the lees in the barrel
Turning the bottles in their racks
Topping up the barrel with wine
Toasting the inside of a barrel
Stirring puts the dead yeast back into the wine and makes a white rounder and creamier. Classic for barrel-aged Chardonnay.
Ageing on the lees gives a white wine…
A creamier texture and bready notes
A sharper acidity and green notes
A deeper colour and more tannin
A sweeter taste and less alcohol
The yeast cells slowly break down and release compounds that add body and aromas of bread, biscuit and brioche.
Autolysis, which gives Champagne its brioche notes, is the breakdown of…
Dead yeast cells in the bottle
The longer a sparkling wine rests on its lees before disgorgement, the more toast, biscuit and brioche it shows.
Turns a sharp acid into a softer one
Malic acid, sharp like a green apple, becomes lactic acid, soft like milk. The wine feels rounder and less tart.
Which aroma in a Chardonnay is a typical sign of malolactic conversion?
The process produces diacetyl, the compound that makes butter smell of butter. Hence the “buttery” Chardonnay.
Lactic bacteria do the work, usually after the yeast has finished. Almost all reds go through it, and some whites.
Cava gets its bubbles in the same way as…
Cava is made by the traditional method: the second fermentation happens in the bottle, as in Champagne.
A second fermentation in a sealed tank
A second fermentation in each bottle
CO2 injected into a still wine
One fermentation that ends in the bottle
The wine is bottled under pressure straight from the tank. It is quicker and cheaper, and keeps fresh fruit aromas.
How does Prosecco usually get its bubbles?
The tank method protects the pear and flower aromas of the Glera grape, so Prosecco tastes fruity, not yeasty.
In the traditional method, what is riddling (remuage)?
Turning bottles to gather yeast in the neck
Freezing the neck to remove the yeast
Adding sugar and yeast to the base wine
Blending base wines from several years
Bottles are tilted and turned little by little until they stand upside down, by hand in racks or by machine.
In the traditional method, what is disgorgement?
Removing the yeast deposit from the bottle
Fitting the cork and the wire cage
The neck is frozen, the cap is taken off and the pressure shoots out the plug of yeast. The wine is left perfectly clear.
In sparkling wine, what is the “dosage”?
Wine and sugar added after disgorgement
Yeast and sugar added to start the bubbles
The share of each grape in the blend
The pressure of the gas in the bottle
The dosage sets the sweetness: none for Brut Nature, a little for Brut, more for Demi-Sec.
The “liqueur de tirage” added to a base wine in the traditional method is…
Sugar and yeast for the second fermentation
Brandy that raises the level of alcohol
Sweet wine that sets the final sweetness
Older reserve wine that adds depth
The yeast eats this sugar inside the sealed bottle. The CO2 it makes has nowhere to go and becomes the bubbles.
How does a pét-nat (ancestral method) get its bubbles?
It is bottled before the first fermentation ends
Sugar and yeast are added to a finished wine
It ferments a second time in a tank
CO2 is injected when it is bottled
Short for “pétillant naturel”: one fermentation, finished in the bottle. It is often cloudy, as the yeast stays inside.
Roughly how much pressure is there inside a bottle of Champagne?
That is two to three times the pressure in a car tyre, which is why you keep a thumb on the cork while opening.
Why is a late-harvest wine sweet?
The grapes stay on the vine and build more sugar
Sugar is stirred in just before bottling
The wine is heated until it thickens
Sweet liqueur is added to a dry wine
Weeks of extra ripening concentrate the sugar, and the yeast cannot ferment it all. The sweetness is the grape’s own.
Which of these wines is made from grapes affected by noble rot?
Sauternes from Bordeaux and Tokaji Aszú from Hungary are the two classic noble-rot wines: honey, apricot, saffron.
What is the scientific name of the fungus behind noble rot?
In wet weather the same fungus is the grey rot that ruins a crop. Only with misty mornings and dry afternoons is it “noble”.
Who proved in the 19th century that living yeast causes fermentation?
Before Pasteur, fermentation was thought to be a purely chemical change. His work made modern, clean winemaking possible.
Ice wine is made from grapes that are…
Frozen on the vine and pressed while frozen
Dried on straw mats for several months
Shrivelled on the vine by noble rot
Picked unripe and stored on ice
The water stays in the press as ice and only a little very sweet juice runs out. Germany and Canada are famous for it.
What is special about the grapes for Amarone?
They are dried for months before pressing
They are left to freeze on the vine
They are picked with noble rot
They are picked before they ripen
Drying concentrates sugar and flavour. Amarone is fermented dry, so it is powerful and high in alcohol, not sweet.
Grape spirit is added to it
It is aged for at least ten years
It is fermented a second time
It is boiled down to concentrate it
The spirit raises the alcohol and makes the wine stable. Port, Sherry, Madeira and Marsala are the classic examples.
Which of these is a fortified wine?
Sauternes is sweet and Amarone is strong, but neither has spirit added. Port does, which takes it to about 20%.
How strong are fortified wines such as Port and Sherry?
They sit between still wine and spirits, which is why they are poured in smaller measures.
Spirit is added to stop the fermentation
Sugar is added after the fermentation
The grapes are dried in the sun first
The grapes are picked with noble rot
Grape spirit is added halfway through. It kills the yeast, so the rest of the grape sugar stays in the wine.
When is the spirit added in making a Fino or Oloroso Sherry?
So these Sherries start as dry wines. Sweet styles such as Cream get their sugar later, from sweet wine blended in.
A film of yeast floating on the wine
A mould that grows on the grapes
A deposit at the bottom of the cask
A spirit used to fortify the wine
Flor shields the wine from air, keeping it pale, and gives Fino its tangy notes of bread dough and almond.
Tiers of casks where young wine refreshes older
A vineyard planted on white chalk soil
A cellar cooled by the sea breeze
A cask kept for a single vintage
Wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest casks, which are topped up from younger ones. So Sherry rarely has a vintage.
What sets Madeira apart from other fortified wines?
It is deliberately heated as it ages
It ages under a layer of flor
It is made from frozen grapes
It ferments a second time in bottle
Heat and air give Madeira its caramel and nut flavours and make it almost indestructible: an open bottle keeps for months.
How does a Tawny Port differ from a Ruby Port?
It is aged much longer in wooden casks
It has much more spirit added
It is made only from white grapes
It is made from sun-dried grapes
Years in cask with a little air turn Tawny amber, with nuts and caramel. Ruby is bottled young: deep red and fruity.
Where does a Vintage Port do most of its ageing?
It is bottled unfiltered after about two years and matures for decades in glass, so it throws sediment and needs decanting.
Pedro Ximénez (PX) Sherry is intensely sweet because the grapes are…
Dried in the sun before pressing
Frozen on the vine in winter
The grapes turn to raisins, so PX is dark and syrupy, with fig, date and molasses. Lovely poured over vanilla ice cream.
What does “organic” on a wine tell you?
A wine with no sulphites at all
A wine that has not been filtered
A wine fermented without any yeast
No synthetic pesticides, herbicides or fertilisers. Organic wines can still contain sulphites, in smaller amounts.
What does biodynamic farming add to organic rules?
A lunar calendar and special composts
A ban on any use of oak barrels
A ban on harvesting grapes by hand
A rule to use only very old vines
The vineyard is treated as one living organism: work follows the moon, and herbal and mineral preparations feed the soil.
Whose ideas from the 1920s are the basis of biodynamic farming?
The Austrian philosopher set out the principles in a series of lectures to farmers in 1924.
Wild yeast and almost nothing added
Any wine made without oak barrels
A wine with the alcohol removed
A wine sweetened only with honey
Usually from organic grapes, with little or no added sulphites and no filtering. There is no single legal definition.
Why are sulphites added to wine?
To raise its level of alcohol
Sulphites are a preservative used for centuries: they guard the wine against oxygen and unwanted yeasts and bacteria.
A wine is made with no added sulphites. Does it contain any?
Yes, a little, made by the yeast
Yes, more than a normal wine
Only if it was aged in oak
Fermentation itself produces small amounts, so no wine is truly sulphite-free. Never promise that to an allergic guest.
Which wines usually contain the most sulphites?
Sugar needs extra protection, so sweet wines get the most. Dry reds need the least: their tannins help to protect them.
Which part of the cork oak is made into wine corks?
The bark is stripped by hand about every nine years and grows back, so the tree is never cut down.
Which wine fault does a screwcap practically rule out?
TCA comes mostly from natural cork. A screwcap is not a sign of a cheap wine: many top producers choose it.
How does the colour of a white wine change as it ages?
It deepens, from lemon to gold and amber
It fades, from gold to almost clear
It turns green, from lemon to lime
It turns pink, from lemon to salmon
Whites darken and reds grow paler with age. A young white that is already deep gold may be oxidised or oak-aged.
Most of the world’s wines are made to be drunk…
Within a few years of the harvest
After at least ten years in a cellar
Only after five years in barrel
Twenty years or more after bottling
Only a small share of wines improve with long cellaring. For most, older does not mean better.
Which wine is most likely to improve over twenty years in bottle?
Tannin, acidity and sugar are what preserve a wine. Light, fruity wines are at their best young.
Why does a wine age more slowly in a magnum than in a standard bottle?
There is less air for each litre of wine
The glass is thicker and keeps it colder
The cork is always a synthetic one
More sulphites are added at bottling
The neck and cork are the same size but there is twice the wine, so it matures more slowly and often more evenly.
Which part of the grape holds most of its juice and sugar?
The pulp gives juice, sugar and acid; the skins give colour, aroma and tannin; seeds and stems give bitter tannin.
What does “dry” mean when we describe a wine?
It dries the mouth with tannin
It was aged in oak barrels
Dry is about sugar, not the drying grip of tannin. A dry wine can still be very fruity.
Which part of a red wine dries and grips your gums and tongue?
Tannin feels like strong black tea left too long. It softens with age, with air and with food.
After a sip your mouth waters and the wine feels fresh. What is high in it?
Acidity is the freshness of a wine. To a guest we say “fresh” or “crisp”, never “sour”.
What does the “body” of a wine describe?
How light or heavy it feels in the mouth
How long the taste lasts after a sip
How sweet or dry it tastes
A light wine slips down like water, a full-bodied one feels thicker and weightier in the mouth.
Which word describes what lingers in the mouth after you swallow?
We call it short, medium or long. Count the seconds the flavour stays with you after the sip.
The flavour of a wine lingers for a long time after you swallow. This usually points to…
A wine that is too young
A wine with a lot of sugar
Length is one of the classic marks of quality, together with balance, intensity and complexity.
A guest wants a white that is “fruity but not sweet”. What do you look for?
A dry wine with ripe fruit aromas
An off-dry wine with low acidity
A dessert wine served very cold
A neutral wine with little aroma
Fruity is what we smell, sweet is the sugar we taste. Many dry wines smell of ripe peach or mango.
It has a slight, gentle sweetness
It has no sugar left at all
It is as sweet as a dessert wine
It is dry, but low in alcohol
Off-dry wines calm spicy food and suit guests who find bone-dry wines too sharp.
The “legs” or “tears” running down the inside of a glass are a sign of…
Thick, slow legs mean a richer wine, not a better one. It is a common myth at the table.
A wine is described as “mineral”. Which notes does the taster mean?
Minerality is a stony, slightly salty freshness, typical of crisp whites from cool places.
What do we mean when we call a wine “balanced”?
It is a blend of several grapes
It is neither young nor old
In a balanced wine the fruit, acidity, tannin, alcohol and sweetness sit together and none dominates.
How do you feel high alcohol when you taste a wine?
As a drying grip on the gums
As a prickle on the tip of the tongue
A wine with too much alcohol for its fruit tastes “hot”. Serving it a little cooler helps.
In which order do we assess a wine?
The eye checks clarity and colour, the nose finds most of the flavour and any fault, the mouth confirms.
Why do we swirl wine in the glass before smelling it?
Swirling brings air into the wine and lifts the aromas. This is why a glass is filled only to a third.
“Tertiary” aromas such as leather, mushroom and dried fruit come from…
Primary aromas come from the grape, secondary from the winemaking, tertiary from time in barrel and bottle.
What keeps a very sweet wine from tasting heavy and sticky?
The great sweet wines are also very fresh: the acidity cleans the mouth after the sugar.
A red wine is described as “round”. What does that mean?
Round wines have ripe fruit and soft tannins. They are the safe choice for a guest who asks for a “smooth” red.
A very high level of alcohol
A blend of many grape varieties
A long time in new oak barrels
A complex wine keeps showing something new with every sip. A simple one says one thing and stops.
What adds most to the body of a dry wine?
The higher the alcohol, the fuller a wine feels. Sugar and tannin add weight too, while acidity makes it feel lighter.
A young wine is described as “closed”. What does that mean?
It shows little aroma for now
It is still sealed with its cork
A closed wine usually opens with air: decant it or give it time in a large glass.
A red wine has turned brick-orange at the rim of the glass. What does that suggest?
Young reds are purple or ruby. With age the colour fades towards garnet and brick.
Wines poured from light to full
Several wines of the same year side by side make a “horizontal” tasting.
In tasting, what is the “attack” of a wine?
The first impression in the mouth
The burn of a high alcohol level
Tasters describe a sip in three steps: the attack, the middle of the palate and the finish.
A wine is “corked”. Where does its musty smell come from?
A mould compound (TCA) in the cork
Crumbs of cork floating in the wine
A dry cork that let air in
A cork pushed out by heat
Cork taint has nothing to do with cork crumbs. TCA makes a wine smell of damp cellar and kills its fruit.
The guest tastes the wine and it is clearly corked. What do you do?
Take it away and open another bottle
Decant it so the smell blows off
Chill it well and pour it again
Leave it open for ten minutes
Cork taint never goes away with air or cold, it only gets clearer. Apologise and replace the bottle.
What colour does a white wine turn when it has oxidised?
Like a cut apple left in the air, an oxidised white goes dark and loses its fresh fruit.
A young white smells of bruised apple and stale nuts and tastes flat. The fault is…
Too much air has reached the wine, through a poor cork or a bottle left open too long.
A just-opened wine smells of rotten egg or burnt rubber. This is called…
Reduction is the opposite of oxidation: the wine had too little air and formed sulphur smells.
A freshly opened wine has a light smell of sulphur. What often clears it?
Rest: an hour with the cork in
Warmth: a few minutes in the hand
Light reduction blows off with air in a few minutes. If the smell stays, treat the bottle as faulty.
A wine smells of vinegar and nail-varnish remover. Which fault is it?
Bacteria have turned some of the alcohol into acetic acid, the acid of vinegar. It does not blow off: replace the bottle.
A bottle that was left in a hot car or next to the oven ends up tasting of…
Heat “cooks” a wine: it turns jammy, flat and tired. This is why bottles never stand near the kitchen or in the sun.
Which sign on an unopened bottle suggests that it got too hot?
A cork pushed up, with wine seeping out
Small clear crystals at the bottom
A deep dent in the base of the bottle
Fine sediment lying along the side
Wine expands when it is hot and forces the cork out. Check the capsule for sticky stains before you present a bottle.
Small clear crystals lie at the bottom of a glass of white wine. What are they?
Tartrates are harmless and tasteless, sometimes called “wine diamonds”. Reassure the guest and pour carefully.
What makes tartrate crystals form in a bottle of wine?
The bottle stood in strong light
Tartaric acid falls out as crystals in the cold, for example after days in a very cold fridge.
What is the dark sediment in an old bottle of red wine made of?
With age, tannin and colour bind together and sink. It is natural, but gritty and bitter, so we decant.
A red wine smells of stable, horse sweat and sticking plaster. The cause is…
TCA, a compound from the cork
Oxygen, let in by a poor cork
“Brett” lives in cellars and barrels. Some guests accept a trace of it, but a strong smell is a fault.
What is the surest way to check a freshly opened bottle for cork taint?
Smell the wine in a glass
Smell the end of the cork
Look at the colour of the cork
Squeeze the cork in your fingers
A cork can smell fine while the wine is tainted, and the other way round. Only the wine tells the truth.
A lightly corked wine may not smell musty. What gives it away?
Muted fruit and a short, flat taste
A light fizz on the tongue
A brown tinge at the rim
At low levels TCA simply strips the aroma. If a wine you know seems dull and lifeless, compare it with another bottle.
Why does the guest who ordered taste the wine before it is poured for the table?
To check that it has no fault
To decide whether they like the style
To give the wine time to breathe
To confirm the vintage on the label
The sip is a check for faults and for temperature, not a trial of whether the choice was a good one.
Crumbs of cork fall into a guest’s glass as you pour. What do you do?
Bring a clean glass and pour again
Say the wine is corked and remove it
Fish them out with a spoon at the table
Leave them: they sink on their own
Cork crumbs are harmless and do not mean the wine is corked, but no guest should have to drink around them.
Why do we keep a corked bottle instead of pouring it away?
The fault fades after a few days
It can be sold by the glass later
The guest may want to take it home
Put the cork back in, mark the bottle and tell the manager: most suppliers give credit for faulty bottles.
A guest insists that a wine is faulty, but it seems fine to you. What do you do?
Do not argue: call the floor manager
Explain that the wine is in good condition
Ask the other guests at the table to judge
Pour a second glass for them to try again
Never argue about taste at the table. The manager decides what happens to the bottle, you keep the guest at ease.
In an old bottle the wine level has dropped well below the neck. What is the risk?
The wine may be too young
The wine may have turned sweet
A low level means wine has escaped and air has taken its place. Tell the manager before you present the bottle.
Why are most wine bottles made of dark glass?
To protect the wine from light
Light spoils wine, fastest of all sparkling and white wine in clear glass. Keep bottles out of the sun and away from spotlights.
A white wine spoiled by heat and air, brown and tasting of cooked nuts, is called…
The word comes from Madeira, a wine that is heated on purpose. In an ordinary white it is a fault of bad storage.
Why do we hold a wine glass by the stem?
So the hand does not warm the wine
So the glass is harder to break
So the wine stays still in the bowl
It also keeps the bowl free of fingerprints. Staff carry and set glasses by the stem or the base only.
Why does a wine glass narrow towards the rim?
The wide bowl lets the wine breathe and the narrower rim holds the aromas where the nose can find them.
Why is a glass for red wine usually bigger than one for white?
More air reaches the wine and opens it
Red wine is poured in larger measures
Red wine has to stay colder
A smaller glass also keeps a white cool for longer. The pour is the same 150 ml in both.
What is a tall, narrow flute good at?
The small surface loses gas slowly and shows a fine stream of bubbles. The price is less aroma.
Why do many sommeliers pour fine Champagne into a tulip or white wine glass?
The wider bowl shows more aroma
The wine keeps its bubbles longer
The glass holds a bigger pour
A complex sparkling wine is still a wine: it needs some room to open, which a narrow flute does not give.
Which red is the wide, balloon-shaped “Burgundy” glass made for?
The big bowl catches the delicate perfume of light, aromatic reds. Tannic reds go in the taller Bordeaux glass.
Why is dessert wine served in a small glass?
It is poured in small measures
It has to warm up quickly
It needs a lot of air
Sweet wines are rich and intense, so a small, cold pour is enough. A large glass would warm it too soon.
Before a glass goes on the table, why do we smell it?
To catch detergent or cupboard smells
To tell crystal from ordinary glass
To check that it is cold enough
To see whether it held red or white
A glass that smells of anything will make every wine smell of it. Hold it to the light for marks, too.
What snaps most stems when wine glasses are polished?
Twisting the base against the bowl
Using a cloth that is too soft
Polishing while the glass is warm
Holding the bowl inside the cloth
Hold the bowl, not the base, while you polish the bowl. Twisting in opposite directions breaks the stem.
A table moves from a white wine to a red. What happens with the glasses?
Clean glasses are set for the red
The red goes on top of the last white
The glasses are rinsed with water at the table
The same glasses are wiped with a napkin
Every new wine gets its own clean glass of the right shape, so nothing of the last wine is left in it.
What does it mean to “season” a glass or a decanter?
Rinse it with a little of the wine
Polish it with a steamed cloth
Chill it with ice before use
Warm it briefly in hot water
A splash of the same wine, swirled and poured out, removes any trace of water, dust or detergent.
A shallow silver cup for tasting
A basket for carrying old bottles
A knife for cutting the capsule
Its shiny dimples show a wine’s colour in a dark cellar. Today it is mostly the badge of the sommelier.
A blended Scotch whisky is a mix of…
A blend marries flavourful malts with lighter grain whisky, often from dozens of distilleries, for a smooth and steady style.
What does “single grain” mean on a Scotch whisky?
From one distillery, using corn or wheat
From one single kind of grain, unmixed
From one single cask, never blended
From one single run of a column still
