“Single” means one distillery, as in single malt. Grain whisky is lighter and is the backbone of most blends.
Malts from several distilleries, no grain whisky
Malt and grain whisky from one distillery
Malt whisky mixed with grain whisky
Malts of different ages from one distillery
Once called “vatted malt”. Monkey Shoulder is a well-known example: all malt, but not from a single distillery.
What does “single cask” on a whisky label tell you?
Every bottle was filled from one cask
It was distilled one single time
It is made from one barley variety
It was aged for one year only
No blending between casks, so each bottling is unique and limited: a few hundred bottles, often at cask strength.
What does “cask strength” on a whisky mean?
Bottled undiluted, as strong as in the cask
Aged in extra-strong new oak casks
Distilled three times for more power
Aged twice as long as usual
Most whisky is cut with water to 40–46% before bottling. Cask strength is often 55–60%: offer water on the side.
A non-chill-filtered whisky may turn hazy with ice or water. Why?
Its natural oils cloud when cold
Its live yeast wakes up again
Chill filtering removes those oils for a clear look, but many feel it also takes away texture and flavour. The haze is harmless.
A whisky is described as “NAS”. What does that tell you?
No age is stated on the label
NAS is “no age statement”. The blender is free to mix young and old casks; by itself it says nothing about quality.
Laphroaig, Lagavulin and Ardbeg come from which Scotch whisky region?
The three stand side by side on the south coast of Islay and are the classic smoky, medicinal, sea-salty malts.
Which Scotch region has the most distilleries and is known for fruity, elegant malts?
Dozens of distilleries sit along the river Spey, more than anywhere else in Scotland, among them Glenfiddich, The Glenlivet and The Macallan.
Lowland malts such as Auchentoshan are traditionally…
Lowland whisky is the gentle side of Scotch, often triple distilled: a good first malt for a guest who fears smoke.
Springbank comes from which Scotch whisky region?
Campbeltown, on the Kintyre peninsula, once had over thirty distilleries. Today a handful remain, known for oily, briny malts.
What do sherry casks typically give a whisky?
Think raisins, figs, walnuts and Christmas cake, plus a deeper amber colour. The Macallan and GlenDronach are classic sherried malts.
Which notes are typical of a Scotch aged in ex-bourbon casks?
American white oak is rich in vanilla-like aromas and gives a paler, golden whisky than a sherry cask does.
Why are used bourbon barrels so plentiful for ageing Scotch?
Bourbon may only be aged in new barrels
Bourbon is aged for only a few weeks
Bourbon barrels are made in Scotland
Bourbon moves to steel tanks after a year
Each new charred oak barrel holds bourbon only once. Then many are shipped to Scotland, Ireland, the Caribbean and Mexico.
A whisky label says “port cask finish”. What does it mean?
It ended its ageing in port casks
A little port wine was added at bottling
It was distilled from port wine
It was aged in the city of Porto
After its main years in bourbon or sherry wood, the whisky moves to a second cask for an extra layer: here red fruit and sweetness.
What colour is whisky when it comes off the still?
All the colour of a whisky, a cognac or an aged rakia comes from the years in wood, sometimes helped by a little caramel.
Jameson and most Irish whiskeys are distilled…
Triple distillation gives the light, smooth style Irish whiskey is known for. Most Scotch malt is distilled twice.
What sets Irish “single pot still” whiskey apart?
It uses malted and unmalted barley
It is made only from corn
It is dried over peat smoke
It is made in a column still
The raw barley gives a creamy, spicy character. Redbreast and Green Spot are the best-known examples.
Which US state is the historic home of bourbon?
Bourbon may be made anywhere in the USA, but the great majority still comes from Kentucky: Maker’s Mark, Woodford Reserve, Buffalo Trace.
Japanese whisky was modelled on the whisky of which country?
Masataka Taketsuru learned the craft in Scotland around 1920 and brought it home. Japanese malts are made the Scottish way.
Mizunara, prized for some Japanese whisky casks, is…
Mizunara oak is rare, porous and hard to work. It gives notes of sandalwood, incense and coconut.
Which sherry cask gives a whisky its sweetest, most raisin-like notes?
Pedro Ximénez (PX) is a syrupy sherry from sun-dried grapes. Its casks give raisins, dates and treacle; Oloroso casks are drier and nuttier.
A 12-year-old whisky spends ten more years in its bottle. How old is it now?
Spirits mature only in the cask. Glass is neutral, so the age on the label never changes, unlike a wine that develops in bottle.
Spirit that evaporates from the cask
The first glass from a new bottle
Spirit kept back for the owner
The sediment left in an old cask
A cask loses a little every year through the wood, more in hot climates. It is one reason old spirits are rare and costly.
Compared with a column still, a copper pot still gives a spirit that is…
Pot stills work batch by batch and keep more flavour: malt whisky, cognac, rakia. Columns run non-stop and give lighter spirit: vodka, grain whisky.
Which part of a distillation run becomes the finished spirit?
The residue left in the still
The heads are harsh and contain methanol, the tails are oily and dull. The distiller’s skill lies in where to make the cuts.
Why are stills for fine spirits made of copper?
Copper reacts with the sulphur from fermentation, so the spirit smells clean and fruity instead of eggy. It also conducts heat well.
What must happen to fruit or grain before it can be distilled?
Distilling does not create alcohol, it only concentrates what the yeast has already made. Whisky starts as a kind of beer, cognac as wine.
How should a corked bottle of whisky or cognac be stored?
Strong alcohol eats away at the cork if it stays in contact, so spirits stand up. Wine lies down, to keep its cork moist.
Which glass is best for nosing a fine whisky served neat?
The narrowing rim gathers the aromas at the nose, as in a wine glass. The Glencairn is the best-known shape. A tumbler suits whisky with ice.
Why do good bars serve whisky over one large ice cube?
It melts slowly and dilutes less
It chills far more than small cubes
It adds minerals to the whisky
It makes the whisky smell stronger
Less surface for the same amount of ice means slower melting, so the drink stays cold without turning watery.
Which order of cognac grades runs from youngest to oldest?
VS is the young, lively one; VSOP is rounder; XO is the long-aged one for slow sipping. The grade shows the youngest spirit in the blend.
Which grape is the backbone of cognac?
Ugni Blanc (Trebbiano in Italy) gives a thin, sharp, low-alcohol wine: poor to drink, perfect to distil.
The Charentais pot still is heated over a flame and the wine goes through it twice, which gives cognac its finesse.
How does armagnac traditionally differ from cognac?
It is never aged in oak
One pass through a small column still leaves more flavour in the spirit: armagnac is more rustic and robust, cognac more polished.
Calvados is a brandy made from…
Cider from Normandy is distilled and then aged in oak. Young calvados smells of fresh apple, older ones of baked apple and spice.
What does “Fine Champagne” on a cognac label mean?
A blend of the two best cognac districts
A cognac blended with champagne wine
A cognac aged in champagne cellars
A cognac made from champagne grapes
Grande Champagne and Petite Champagne are the top areas of Cognac, named for their chalky soil. Nothing to do with sparkling wine.
How is a fine old cognac classically served?
Over crushed ice, in a tumbler
Chilled from the freezer, as a shot
Topped up with soda and lemon
Cold and ice hide the aromas that took decades to build. The warmth of the hand is enough: no heating over a flame.
Pomace is the skins, seeds and stalks left after the wine is pressed. Grappa is Italian; its Bulgarian cousin is dzhibrova rakia.
Pisco is a grape brandy from…
Both countries claim it as their national spirit. It is usually clear and unaged, with a floral, grapey aroma, close to a grape rakia.
The “trou normand”, a pause in the middle of a long meal, is a small glass of…
The “Norman hole”: a sip of calvados, today often poured over apple sorbet, to make room for the dishes still to come.
Most rum is made from molasses. Agricole, the pride of Martinique, uses fresh juice and tastes grassier, drier and more vegetal.
Cachaça, a sugar cane spirit, comes from…
Like rhum agricole it is made from fresh cane juice, not molasses. It is the spirit of the Caipirinha.
Which island is famous for heavy, pungent pot-still rums?
Long fermentation and pot stills give Jamaican rum its “funk”: overripe banana, pineapple and spice. Cuban-style rum is light and clean.
Molasses, the base of most rum, is…
The dark syrup left from sugar making
The fresh juice pressed from the cane
The dried leaves of the sugar cane
The burnt sugar used for colouring
Once the sugar crystals are taken out, a thick, dark, bittersweet syrup remains. Fermented and distilled, it becomes rum.
What does “London Dry” on a gin tell you?
It is a dry style, made anywhere
It was aged in oak in London
London Dry can be made in any country. All the flavour comes from distilling with the botanicals; no flavourings or colour are added afterwards.
After juniper, which botanical is the most common in gin?
Coriander seed gives a citrusy, spicy lift. Angelica root and citrus peel complete the classic gin recipe.
Sloe gin gets its red colour and its flavour from…
The sloes are steeped in gin with sugar, so it is really a liqueur: sweet-tart, plummy, and lower in alcohol than gin.
Genever, the malty ancestor of gin, comes from…
English soldiers met genever in the Low Countries and shortened its name to “gin”. It tastes maltier, closer to a young whisky.
Wheat and rye are the classics, potatoes a Polish speciality. Wheat vodkas feel soft, rye ones spicier, potato ones creamier.
Why does vodka taste so neutral?
It is distilled very pure and filtered
It is aged in old, neutral casks
It is made from water and sugar only
It is bottled weaker than other spirits
Column stills take it to around 96% alcohol, stripping out almost all flavour, and charcoal filtering polishes it further.
Bottled straight after distilling, blanco shows the pure taste of agave: pepper, citrus and green, earthy notes.
Which of these tequilas has spent the longest in oak?
Añejo means “aged”: at least a year in small oak casks. Reposado, “rested”, gets a few months. Añejo is sipped like a cognac, not as a shot.
The agave is roasted in earth pits
The spirit is aged in charred casks
The spirit is filtered through charcoal
The agave is dried over peat fires
The agave hearts cook for days under earth, over hot stones and wood embers. For tequila the agave is steamed in ovens, so there is no smoke.
How does mezcal differ from tequila in its raw material?
It may use many kinds of agave
It is made from cactus fruit
It is made from sugar cane
Tequila allows only blue agave. Mezcal uses dozens of kinds, most often Espadín, and wild ones such as Tobalá. Its heartland is Oaxaca.
What does “100% agave” on a tequila guarantee?
No water was added at bottling
No ageing in oak took place
A tequila without this line (a “mixto”) may get up to about half of its alcohol from cane or corn sugar. For sipping, choose 100% agave.
How would you explain rakia to a foreign guest?
A fruit brandy, distilled from ripe fruit
A grain spirit, similar to a vodka
A sweet liqueur made with fruit and sugar
A fortified wine with added spirit
Grapes and plums are the classics, then apricot, quince, pear. Close relatives: grappa, slivovitz and French eau-de-vie.
At which point of a traditional Bulgarian meal is rakia served?
At the start, with the salad
Rakia is our aperitif: with shopska salad, pickles or cured meats. Many foreign guests expect it as a digestif, so it is worth telling them.
Which part of Bulgaria is famous for apricot rakia?
Silistra and Tutrakan, on the Danube
Troyan and Teteven, in the Balkan range
Melnik and Sandanski, by the Struma
The Danube lowlands of the north-east are apricot country. Troyan and Teteven, in the mountains, mean plum.
Sungurlare, Karnobat and Pomorie are best known for rakia made from…
South-eastern Bulgaria, towards the Black Sea, is vine country: its grape and muscat rakias are aromatic and soft.
It was distilled a second time
It was aged in toasted oak
It was made from baked fruit
The second run through the still gives a cleaner, stronger rakia, often 50% or more. It should be sipped slowly.
Which Hungarian spirit is a close cousin of rakia?
Pálinka is a pure fruit brandy, most often from plum, apricot or pear, with no added sugar. Unicum is a bitter herbal liqueur.
Ouzo is the national anise spirit of…
Ouzo is sipped slowly with iced water and small plates of seafood, olives and cheese. Much of the best comes from the island of Lesbos.
Which drink is called “lion’s milk” once water is added?
“Aslan sütü” in Turkish: the clear rakı turns milky white with water. It is the classic partner of meze and grilled fish.
How is Bulgarian mastika traditionally served?
Warm, with a spoon of honey
At room temperature, in a snifter
Hot, in a small coffee cup
In the cold the anise oil forms fine white crystals, which mastika lovers look for. In summer it goes well with watermelon.
Greek “mastiha” liqueur from Chios is flavoured with…
The resin “tears” of the mastic tree are gathered only in the south of Chios. The taste is piney and fresh, without the anise of Bulgarian mastika.
Like grappa, it uses what is left after the wine is pressed. Some tsipouro has anise, some none; in Crete the same spirit is called tsikoudia.
Pelinkovac is a bitter herbal liqueur from…
Its base is wormwood, which gives a bittersweet taste. It is served chilled as a digestif, often with a slice of lemon.
Sambuca is classically served with three…
“Con la mosca”, with the fly: three beans for health, happiness and prosperity. Sambuca is a sweet anise liqueur, a digestif.
Lemon peel steeped in spirit with sugar, from the coast around Sorrento and Amalfi. It lives in the freezer and is poured into small chilled glasses.
What makes a drink a liqueur?
It is a spirit, flavoured and sweetened
It is a spirit, aged over ten years
It is a wine, with brandy added
It is a spirit, bottled above 50%
Sugar is what defines a liqueur. Fruit, herbs, nuts, cream or coffee give the flavour; the strength is usually 15–40%.
The almond taste often comes from apricot kernels, but some brands use real almonds: always check for a guest with a nut allergy.
Cointreau and triple sec are liqueurs flavoured with…
Sweet and bitter orange peels are distilled into a clear, strong liqueur: the citrus note of many classic cocktails.
Grand Marnier is an orange liqueur based on…
Bitter orange and cognac make it richer and rounder than triple sec. It is the classic liqueur for crêpes Suzette.
Baileys is made from cream and…
It contains milk, so it matters for a guest with a dairy allergy. Served chilled or over ice, as a dessert in a glass.
Who makes the herbal liqueur Chartreuse?
Made from about 130 plants to a secret recipe. The green one is stronger and more herbal, the yellow milder and sweeter.
In “crème de menthe” or “crème de cacao”, the word “crème” means…
A very sweet liqueur, with no cream
A liqueur made with dairy cream
A liqueur thickened with egg yolk
“Crème” signals a high sugar content and a syrupy texture. Only “cream liqueurs”, such as Baileys, contain dairy.
Advocaat, the thick yellow Dutch liqueur, is made with…
Egg yolks, sugar and brandy: like a custard with alcohol. Remember it for a guest with an egg allergy.
When is an amaro such as Averna or Montenegro usually served?
After the meal, as a digestif
With the main course, like wine
“Amaro” means bitter: the herbs are meant to settle the stomach after a rich dinner. Serve it neat or over ice, sometimes with orange peel.
Aperol is orange in colour and taste and has about 11% alcohol; Campari is red, far more bitter and about twice as strong.
How would you describe Fernet-Branca to a guest?
Very bitter, with menthol and herbs
Very little sugar and a strong medicinal bite make it the most extreme of the amari. Warn a guest who has never tried it.
Which bark gives tonic water and Dubonnet their bitterness?
Cinchona bark contains quinine, once the medicine against malaria. Wine aperitifs made with it are called quinquinas.
What is the purpose of an aperitif?
To wake up the appetite before a meal
To help digestion after a meal
To refresh the palate between dishes
To go with the dessert and coffee
From the Latin “aperire”, to open. Good aperitifs are dry, bitter or sparkling and light: vermouth, a bitter, champagne, dry sherry.
Which of these is a classic digestif?
After the meal come the strong and the sweet: cognac, armagnac, aged rakia, whisky, amaro and liqueurs. The other three open a meal.
The word “vermouth” comes from the German name of which herb?
“Wermut” is wormwood, the bitter herb that defines the drink. The same plant gave absinthe its name too.
How should an opened bottle of vermouth be kept?
In the fridge, for a few weeks
On the shelf, for several years
In the freezer, for a year
In the cellar, lying on its side
Vermouth is wine: once open it oxidises and turns flat and stale. A tired vermouth spoils every drink it goes into.
Classic red vermouth from Turin gets its colour mainly from…
The base is white wine: the red-brown colour comes from caramel, the taste from herbs, spices and sugar.
Which drink is nicknamed the “Green Fairy”?
The drink of the artists of 19th-century Paris, banned for decades and legal again today. Very strong, with anise and herbs, served with iced water.
What kind of drink is sake?
Distilled from rice, like a vodka
Distilled from barley, like a whisky
“Rice wine” is a handy name, but sake is brewed more like a beer, from grain. It is served with food, like wine.
Because it is clear and comes in small cups, guests often take sake for a spirit. Pour it like wine, not like a shot.
What does “junmai” on a sake label mean?
No filtering, so it is cloudy
No water was added at bottling
“Pure rice”: only rice, water, koji and yeast. Junmai sakes tend to be fuller and more savoury, good with food.
In sake, the words “ginjo” and “daiginjo” tell you…
How far the rice was polished
How long the sake was aged
The more of each grain is milled away, the finer and more fragrant the sake. Daiginjo keeps half of the grain or less. Serve it lightly chilled.
What does koji do when sake is made?
It turns the rice starch into sugar
It turns the sugar into alcohol
It filters the sake until clear
It gives the sake its bubbles
Koji is a noble mould grown on steamed rice. Rice has no sugar for the yeast, so koji makes it first; it is also behind miso and soy sauce.
Which spirit goes into a classic Negroni?
A Negroni is gin, Campari and sweet red vermouth in equal parts, stirred and served over ice.
Which bitter liqueur gives a Negroni its red colour?
Campari is an Italian bitter of herbs and bitter orange. Warn the guest: a Negroni is strong and clearly bitter.
A Boulevardier is a Negroni with the gin replaced by…
Bourbon or rye makes it rounder and warmer than a Negroni: a good suggestion for a whiskey drinker.
What is stirred with gin to make a classic Martini?
Only two ingredients, stirred over ice and strained into a chilled glass, with an olive or a lemon twist.
Which spirit is the base of a Manhattan?
The classic recipe uses American rye; bourbon makes a slightly sweeter drink. It is served with a cherry.
Besides whiskey and bitters, what goes into a Manhattan?
The vermouth rounds off the whiskey. The same recipe made with Scotch is called a Rob Roy.
An Old Fashioned is whiskey, a little sugar and…
Spirit, sugar, bitters and ice: one of the oldest cocktail recipes, finished with a strip of orange peel.
Which spirit is the base of a Margarita?
A Margarita is shaken with orange liqueur and fresh lime juice, and often served with salt on the rim.
Which liqueur is shaken with tequila and lime juice in a Margarita?
Triple sec is an orange liqueur; Cointreau is the best-known brand.
Which spirit is the base of a classic Daiquiri?
The Daiquiri was born in Cuba, the home of light rum. It is served “straight up”: cold, with no ice in the glass.
A classic Daiquiri is white rum, sugar and the juice of…
Fresh lime balances the sugar. Fruit versions, such as strawberry, are built on the same three ingredients.
Which herb goes into a Mojito?
The leaves are pressed gently, not shredded: crushed hard, they turn the drink bitter.
Which spirit is the base of a Caipirinha?
Cachaça is Brazil’s sugar-cane spirit. It is poured over lime and sugar crushed right in the glass.
In an Aperol Spritz, what is the Aperol mixed with?
It is built over ice in a large wine glass and finished with a slice of orange.
What gives a Whiskey Sour its silky foam on top?
The egg white is optional, and egg is an allergen: always tell the guest. Without it there is no foam.
Which spirit is the base of an Espresso Martini?
It is shaken hard with coffee liqueur and a fresh espresso. Despite the name, it has no vermouth.
Which juice gives a Cosmopolitan its pink colour?
A Cosmopolitan is citrus vodka, orange liqueur, lime and a little cranberry juice, served in a cocktail glass.
Which sauce is a classic seasoning of a Bloody Mary?
It joins vodka, tomato juice, lemon, Tabasco, salt and pepper. Worcestershire contains anchovies: fish is an allergen.
A Mimosa is sparkling wine mixed with…
A brunch classic served in a flute. In Britain the same mix is known as a Buck’s Fizz.
A Bellini is Prosecco mixed with a purée of…
It was created at Harry’s Bar in Venice. With strawberry purée the drink is called a Rossini.
A Kir is dry white wine with a little…
The liqueur is crème de cassis. The drink comes from Burgundy, where it was traditionally made with Aligoté.
What turns a Kir into a Kir Royal?
A dash of cognac on top
A sugar rim on the glass
The same crème de cassis, topped with Champagne or another dry sparkling wine and served in a flute.
What is the vodka topped with in a Moscow Mule?
With lime, over ice, traditionally in a copper mug. The ginger beer used at the bar is a spicy soft drink.
Tequila, lime and grapefruit soda over ice, often with a salted rim: a very popular long drink in Mexico.
What is the glass rinsed with before a Sazerac is poured in?
A New Orleans classic: a few drops coat the chilled glass and leave an anise scent over the drink.
A Cuba Libre is cola, lime and…
The lime is what separates a Cuba Libre from a plain rum and cola.
Which spirit goes into a Tom Collins?
Gin, lemon juice, sugar and soda water over ice in a tall glass: a fresh long drink for a warm evening.
Besides rum, which two flavours make a Piña Colada?
The name is Spanish for “strained pineapple”. The drink comes from Puerto Rico.
Which syrup gives a Mai Tai its almond note?
Orgeat is made from almonds, so a Mai Tai is not for a guest with a nut allergy.
What makes the red layer at the bottom of a Tequila Sunrise?
Grenadine is a heavy, sweet syrup: poured in last, it sinks through the orange juice.
Which cocktails are normally stirred rather than shaken?
Those with egg white for foam
Stirring keeps a Martini or a Negroni clear and silky. Juice, egg and cream need a hard shake to blend.
What does it mean to “muddle” at the bar?
To press fruit or herbs in the glass
To pour one liquid gently over another
To rub the rim of the glass with citrus
To pass the drink through a fine sieve
Pressing releases the juice and the aromatic oils: the lime in a Caipirinha, the mint in a Mojito.
A drink that is “built” is made…
Straight in the glass it is served in
In a blender with crushed ice
In a mixing glass, then strained
Ice first, then the spirit, then the mixer: this is how a gin and tonic or an Aperol Spritz is made.
Why is a shaken cocktail “double strained” through a fine sieve?
To catch ice chips and bits of fruit
To cool the drink a second time
To make the drink less strong
Small shards of ice would go on melting and water the drink down; pulp and herb pieces spoil the texture.
Ice in the shaker chills the drink. What else does it do?
The melted water is part of the recipe: it softens the alcohol and brings the flavours together.
Pour it gently so it stays on top
Shake it with all the other ingredients
Freeze it into the ice cubes
Stir it in until it disappears
It is poured over the back of a spoon: the cream on an Irish Coffee, the dark rum on a Dark ’n’ Stormy.
A guest asks for a Martini “extra dry”. What do they want?
No ice used in making it
In a Martini, “dry” describes the amount of vermouth: the drier the order, the closer to pure chilled gin.
The brine makes the drink cloudy and salty. It is garnished with olives.
A drink ordered “with a twist” comes with…
The peel is squeezed over the glass so that its oils perfume the surface of the drink.
A tall drink with plenty of mixer
A double measure of neat spirit
A cocktail aged in a barrel
A strong short drink without ice
A long drink is lighter in alcohol per sip and is drunk slowly: a good suggestion before dinner or on a hot day.
In bar language, a “sour” is a spirit shaken with…
Whiskey Sour, Pisco Sour and Daiquiri all follow the same idea: strong, sour and sweet in balance.
A guest orders a whisky with ice “on the side”. What do you bring?
The whisky and the ice separately
The whisky poured over the ice
The whisky with one large cube in it
The whisky chilled, without any ice
“On the side” means the guest adds it to taste. The same goes for water or a mixer.
Chilled, in a stemmed glass, without ice
Over ice, in a short tumbler
In a tall glass, with a straw
At room temperature, in a shot glass
The drink is shaken or stirred with ice and then strained: Martini, Manhattan and Daiquiri are served this way.
What does a highball glass look like?
It takes a spirit with plenty of ice and mixer: whisky and soda, Cuba Libre, Mojito.
Which glass is known as an “Old Fashioned glass”?
It is also called a rocks glass: for spirits over ice and short stirred drinks such as the Negroni.
A small two-sided measure for spirits
A long spoon for stirring drinks
A strainer that fits the shaker
A wooden stick for pressing fruit
It keeps every drink the same strength and the stock count honest. The stick for pressing fruit is called a muddler.
A Martini garnished with a pickled cocktail onion is called a…
The recipe is the same gin and dry vermouth: only the garnish changes the name.
What is the classic garnish of a Bloody Mary?
Celery is one of the 14 allergens, and the drink is often seasoned with celery salt as well.
What turns a Black Russian into a White Russian?
Both are vodka and coffee liqueur over ice; the cream is floated on top. Remember that milk is an allergen.
The cocktail called Americano is Campari, sweet vermouth and…
A light, bitter aperitif that has nothing to do with coffee. With gin in place of the soda it becomes a Negroni.
Prosecco, elderflower syrup, mint and soda over ice: lighter and sweeter than an Aperol Spritz, with no bitterness.
A French 75 is gin, lemon and sugar, topped with…
It is named after a French 75 mm field gun of the First World War. Topped with soda instead, it would be a Tom Collins.
What sits on top of an Irish Coffee?
A layer of lightly whipped cream
A cap of steamed milk foam
A scoop of vanilla ice cream
A spoon of beaten egg white
Hot coffee, Irish whiskey and sugar are drunk through the cool cream, so the drink is not stirred.
What gives a Long Island Iced Tea its tea-like colour?
There is no tea in it. Vodka, gin, white rum, tequila and orange liqueur make it a very strong long drink.
Which spirit is the base of a Mint Julep?
Bourbon, mint, sugar and crushed ice in a frosted metal cup: the drink of the Kentucky Derby.
A Dark ’n’ Stormy is ginger beer with…
The dark rum is poured last and sits on the pale ginger beer like a storm cloud, which gave the drink its name.
What separates a lager from an ale?
Lager yeast works cool and slowly, for a clean, crisp beer; ale yeast works warmer and gives fruitier flavours.
What do hops give a beer?
Hops balance the sweetness of the malt. Their aromas run from herbs and flowers to citrus and tropical fruit.
Where does a dark beer get its colour?
The darker the malt is roasted, the more caramel, coffee and chocolate notes. Dark does not mean stronger.
Which allergen is found in almost every beer?
Beer is brewed from barley or wheat malt, both cereals with gluten. A coeliac guest needs a beer labelled gluten-free.
What is an IPA (India Pale Ale) best known for?
A lot of hops: bitter and aromatic
A lot of wheat: cloudy and soft
Expect citrus, pine or tropical fruit on the nose and a firm bitter finish: say so before a guest orders one.
Which beer style is black, with flavours of roasted coffee and dark chocolate?
A stout is a dark ale, often with a thick creamy head. It goes well with chocolate desserts and with oysters.
A German Weissbier is brewed with a large share of…
It is cloudy from the yeast, soft and lightly sweet, with typical aromas of banana and clove.
What ferments a Belgian lambic beer?
Champagne yeast, added in the bottle
The brew is left open to the air near Brussels and ferments by itself. The result is dry and sour; gueuze and kriek are lambics.
How do you start pouring a beer into a glass?
With the glass tilted, down its side
With the glass upright, into the middle
From high above, to build foam
Over a spoon, as slowly as possible
Tilt the glass, pour down the side, then straighten it at the end for a neat head: the foam holds in aroma and gas.
How does a ristretto differ from a normal espresso?
Less water: shorter and more intense
A double dose of coffee and water
A little milk foam on top
Ristretto means “restricted” in Italian. Its opposite is the lungo, where more water runs through the same coffee.
Hot water is added to an espresso
Extra water is run through the coffee
Coffee drips through a paper filter
An espresso is topped with warm milk
That keeps it cleaner and less bitter than a lungo, which pushes more water through the same grounds.
An espresso macchiato is an espresso with…
Macchiato means “stained”: the coffee is only marked with milk. A latte macchiato is the reverse: milk marked with coffee.
Compared with a cappuccino, a caffè latte has…
A latte is the mildest and milkiest. A cappuccino is smaller, with a thick cap of foam and more coffee taste.
What is “flat” about a flat white?
The milk: a thin layer of fine foam
Smaller than a latte, with velvety milk and no thick cap of foam, so the coffee comes through more strongly.
A cortado is an espresso “cut” with…
The name is Spanish for “cut”: the milk softens the espresso without hiding it. Small, with very little foam.
What is the “crema” of an espresso?
The milk added at the end
The grounds left in the cup
The cream served on the side
It forms when hot water under pressure meets freshly roasted coffee. Serve an espresso at once, before it fades.
How does a dark roast taste next to a light roast?
Long roasting brings out bitter, smoky and chocolate notes; a light roast keeps the bean’s own fruit and acidity.
How much caffeine is there in decaffeinated coffee?
Decaffeination removes almost all of the caffeine, not every bit. Tell a guest “almost none”, never “zero”.
An espresso that runs through too fast usually tastes…
Too fast means under-extracted: the water had no time to take the sweetness. Too slow gives a bitter, harsh cup.
What makes black tea different from green tea?
The leaves are oxidised before drying
It comes from a different plant
The leaves are smoked over wood
It is made from older leaves
Both come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis. Oxidation turns the leaf dark and the taste malty and strong.
Oolong sits between green and black tea because its leaves are…
Lightly oxidised oolongs are floral and fresh, close to a green tea; darker ones are toasty and rich.
Which of these contains no caffeine?
Herbal infusions such as chamomile, mint or linden are not made from the tea plant, so they suit a late evening.
Why is green tea brewed with water well below boiling?
Boiling water takes away the colour
Water at around 70–80 °C keeps it fresh and sweet. Black tea and herbal infusions take water just off the boil.
Green tea leaves ground to a powder
The powder is whisked into hot water, so the whole leaf is drunk: more colour, body and caffeine than a steeped tea.
Plain sparkling water, with no sugar
Sparkling water with quinine and sugar
Sparkling water with ginger and sugar
Sparkling water with lemon and sugar
Soda only lengthens a drink and adds bubbles. Unlike tonic, it brings no sweetness and no flavour of its own.
Compared with ginger ale, ginger beer tastes…
Ginger ale is the gentle one, good with whisky. Ginger beer has the bite that a Moscow Mule needs.
A cocktail with half the alcohol
It is also ordered as “virgin”: a Virgin Mojito is a Mojito without the rum. Offer one to drivers and pregnant guests.
It is lightly sour and fizzy. Fermentation can leave a trace of alcohol, which matters to a guest who avoids it completely.
What does “confit” mean for a duck leg?
Cooked slowly in its own fat
Confit is long, gentle cooking submerged in fat. The meat turns very tender and the skin is crisped just before serving.
What was confit first invented for?
To preserve meat under a layer of fat
To make tough meat cook much faster
To remove the fat from rich meat
To give meat a deep smoky flavour
Before fridges, cooked duck or goose kept for months sealed under its own fat. Today it is done for the texture.
In a sealed bag, in a precise warm water bath
Under a salt crust, in a very hot oven
In a sealed pot, under high pressure
Under a glass dome, in cold wood smoke
The low, exact temperature cooks the food evenly from edge to centre and keeps it juicy.
What does the French term “sous-vide” literally mean?
The food is first vacuum-sealed in a bag. The warm water bath that follows is what cooks it.
Why is sous-vide meat usually seared just before serving?
The water bath gives it no browned crust
The centre is still raw after the bath
The bag leaves the surface too salty
The meat comes out of the bath cold
Sous-vide temperatures are too low to brown anything. A few seconds in a very hot pan add colour and roasted flavour.
How has a braised beef cheek been cooked?
Slowly, covered, in a little liquid
Quickly, in a very hot dry pan
Slowly, in dry smoke over wood
Quickly, in plenty of hot oil
Braising means browning the meat, then cooking it for hours in a little stock or wine until it is spoon-tender.
Why are tough cuts like cheek or shank cooked slowly for hours?
Their collagen melts into soft gelatine
Their fibres need time to absorb salt
Their strong smell needs time to fade
Hard-working muscles are full of connective tissue. Long, moist heat turns it into gelatine: hence the rich, sticky texture.
What does “poached” mean, as in poached fish or a poached pear?
Cooked gently in liquid kept below the boil
Fried quickly in a little hot butter
Baked slowly in a dry, low oven
The liquid (water, stock, wine or syrup) only trembles. That gentle heat keeps delicate food moist and whole.
What does it mean to blanch vegetables?
Boil them briefly, then chill them in iced water
Fry them slowly, then drain them on paper
Salt them heavily, then rinse them in water
Roast them whole, then peel off the skin
Blanching fixes a bright colour and leaves a little bite. Green beans and asparagus are the classic examples.
Why do blanched vegetables go straight into iced water?
To stop the cooking and keep the colour
To wash off the salt from the pot
To make them soak up more water
To make them easier to season
Without the ice bath the vegetables keep cooking in their own heat and turn soft and dull.
What does it mean to sear a piece of meat?
Brown its surface fast over very high heat
Cook it slowly, submerged in its own fat
Soak it for hours in salted water
Simmer it gently in a little stock
Searing builds a brown, savoury crust. The inside is then finished more gently, in the pan or in the oven.
Browning of proteins and sugars in dry heat
Setting of egg proteins in a warm custard
Melting of collagen into gelatine in a stew
Souring of dough by wild yeast and bacteria
It is why a seared steak, a bread crust and roasted coffee smell so good. It needs a hot, dry surface.
Coated in a thin, shiny layer of reduced liquid
Covered in a crisp crust of breadcrumbs
Wrapped in pastry and baked until golden
Dusted with flour and fried in deep oil
A glaze is stock, butter, honey or the cooking juices reduced until they cling to the food and shine.
Baked in a sealed paper parcel, in its own steam
Fried in a crust of flour and breadcrumbs
Grilled on a wooden plank over charcoal
Poached slowly in a bath of warm olive oil
The parcel is often opened at the table, so the guest gets the aroma first. The fish stays moist and delicate.
Alcohol is poured over the dish and set alight
The dish is browned under a very hot grill
The dish is cooked over open charcoal
The dish is smoked under a glass dome
The brief flame leaves the aroma of the spirit in the dish. It is often done at the table, as with crêpes Suzette.
To sauté means to cook food…
Quickly, in a little hot fat, tossing it
Slowly, covered, in plenty of liquid
Gently, in steam over boiling water
For hours, in a low and dry oven
From the French “sauter”, to jump: the food jumps in the pan as the cook tosses it.
Browned on top, often with cheese or crumbs
Served cold, set in its own jelly
Cooked sealed in a vacuum bag
Steamed over a pan of stock
The golden crust forms under a hot grill or in the oven. Potato gratin is the best-known example.
What does it mean to deglaze a pan?
Add liquid to dissolve the browned bits
Wipe out the fat before making a sauce
Brush a shiny glaze over the meat
Cool the pan quickly under cold water
Wine or stock lifts the caramelised juices stuck to the pan. They are the base of the best pan sauces.
What does it mean to reduce a sauce?
Simmer it until it thickens and concentrates
Thin it with a little water or stock
Strain it through a very fine cloth
Bind it with a spoonful of flour
As the water evaporates the flavour gets stronger and the sauce turns glossy, with no flour needed.
Seared for seconds, raw inside, then sliced
Cured in salt and sugar for two days
Deep-fried in a light, crisp batter
Simmered slowly in soy sauce and sugar
A Japanese technique: only the outside is cooked. Tell the guest that the centre is raw.
On a flat, very hot metal plate
In a clay pot, in the oven
On a spit, over an open fire
In a basket, over boiling water
The Spanish plancha sears fast with almost no fat, so seafood stays juicy and gets a light crust.
What does baking a whole fish in a salt crust do?
It seals in moisture: the fish steams gently
It cures the flesh until firm and dry
It makes the skin crisp enough to eat
It gives the flesh a light smoky taste
The crust is cracked open and thrown away, often at the table. The flesh is moist and only lightly seasoned.
A bath of hot water for gentle cooking
A bath of iced water for fast chilling
A crust of salt for baking whole fish
A deep pan of oil for frying
Custards are baked in it and sauces like hollandaise are kept warm over it, because the heat never gets harsh.
Floured, fried in butter, with lemon and parsley
Poached in white wine, with a cream sauce
Steamed in a parcel, with herbs and fennel
Grilled over charcoal, with olive oil and salt
“Meunière” means “the miller’s wife”, hence the flour. The butter browns in the pan and becomes the sauce.
Fully raw: sliced thin and dressed cold
Dried hard: salted and hung like ham
French for “half-cooked”. Worth saying at the table, as some guests expect fish to be cooked through.
Cooked through but still firm to the bite
Very soft and almost falling apart
Fried in oil until it turns crisp
Still hard and raw in the middle
Italian for “to the tooth”. The same words are used for risotto rice and for vegetables with a little bite.
In what order is food coated for a classic breadcrumb crust?
The flour dries the surface, the egg glues, the crumbs crisp. So a schnitzel contains gluten and egg.
What does it mean to cure fish or meat?
Preserve it with salt, which draws out water
Cook it slowly in its own melted fat
Boil it briefly and chill it on ice
Coat it in batter and deep-fry it
Salt, often with sugar and spices, pulls out moisture and firms the flesh. Ham, pastarma and gravlax are all cured.
Gravlax is salmon that has been…
Cured with salt, sugar and dill
Poached in white wine and herbs
Marinated in lime juice and chilli
A Scandinavian classic: neither smoked nor cooked. The cure gives the salmon a firm, silky texture.
How does cold-smoked salmon differ from hot-smoked salmon?
It is not cooked by the smoke and stays silky
It is cooked through and flakes apart
It is smoked without being salted first
It is frozen while the smoke is applied
Cold smoke only flavours the cured fish, so it slices thin and silky. Hot smoking cooks it: the flesh is firm and flaky.
What happens when a food ferments?
Microbes turn its sugars into acid or alcohol
Heat breaks its proteins down into sugars
Salt pulls all the water out of the food
Smoke covers the food in a protective layer
Bread, yoghurt, wine, beer and sauerkraut are all the work of friendly yeasts or bacteria.
Why does traditional sauerkraut taste sour?
Bacteria turn its sugars into lactic acid
Vinegar is poured over the cabbage
Lemon juice is added to the brine
The salt turns sour as it ages
Only salt and time are needed. The same lactic fermentation gives kimchi and real sour pickles their tang.
Pickled red onion is a “quick pickle”. What makes it sour?
The onion’s own juice and salt
Vinegar, sugar and salt do the job in minutes or hours, with no fermentation. It adds crunch and freshness to a rich dish.
To marinate meat or fish means to…
Soak it in a seasoned liquid before cooking
Cook it slowly in a sealed vacuum bag
Hang it to dry in cold, moving air
Brush it with a shiny sauce at the end
Oil, acid, herbs and spices flavour the surface, and the acid softens it a little.
Why is chicken or pork soaked in brine before cooking?
It is seasoned through and stays juicier
It cooks through without any heat
It takes on a smoky taste and colour
It loses its fat and becomes lean
The meat absorbs some of the salted water, so it holds more moisture during cooking.
Left in sugar or alcohol to release their juice
Dried slowly in a low oven until chewy
Cooked down with sugar into a thick jam
Frozen hard and grated over the plate
No heat is used: the sugar or liqueur draws out the juice and makes a natural syrup.
What happens to beef during dry ageing?
It loses water, so the flavour concentrates
It soaks in brine, so it stays juicy
It is lightly smoked, so it keeps longer
It is frozen, so the fibres break down
The meat hangs for weeks in cold, moving air. Its own enzymes tenderise it and the taste turns deep and nutty.
Why does dry-aged beef cost more than fresh beef?
It loses weight and its dry crust is cut away
It can only be made from the fillet
It needs costly spices and salt rubs
It has to be cooked for much longer
Weeks in the ageing room, evaporation and trimming: far less meat is left to sell from the same cut.
Wet ageing tenderises without weight loss, so it is cheaper. It does not build the nutty depth of dry ageing.
Why is a steak rested for a few minutes before it is served?
The juices settle and stay in the meat
The crust needs time to turn crisp
The fat needs time to firm up again
The salt needs time to reach the centre
Cut straight from the pan, a steak floods the plate with juice. That is why it takes a few minutes longer than guests expect.
A roast leaves the oven to rest. What happens in its centre?
It keeps cooking and gets a little hotter
It starts to cool down straight away
It stays at exactly the same heat
It cools faster than the outside does
Heat keeps moving from the outside in, so chefs take meat out a little early. Resting is part of the cooking.
Which is the right order, from least cooked to most cooked?
Rare, medium rare, medium, well done
Medium rare, rare, medium, well done
Rare, medium, medium rare, well done
Medium, rare, medium rare, well done
Before rare comes “blue”, and between medium and well done comes “medium well”: the full scale a guest may use.
How do you describe a medium rare steak to a guest?
Cool raw centre, barely seared outside
Grey-brown right through, no pink at all
Only a thin pink line in the middle
It is the doneness most kitchens suggest for a tender cut: juicy, soft and warm all the way through.
A guest asks for a steak “blue”. What do they want?
Seared outside, almost raw and cool inside
Cooked through, with no pink left inside
Pink all through and hot in the centre
Cooked slowly sous-vide and served cold
Blue (French “bleu”) is one step below rare: only a few seconds a side in a very hot pan.
Which French steak term means pink in the centre, between rare and well done?
À point means “at the right point”. Bleu is almost raw, saignant (“bloody”) is rare and bien cuit is well done.
What does “marbling” mean in a steak?
Fine streaks of fat inside the muscle
Dark grill marks across the surface
A thick layer of fat along the edge
The direction of the meat fibres
The fat melts as the steak cooks and makes it juicier and richer. Rib-eye and wagyu are known for it.
Why is duck breast cooked skin-side down first, over gentle heat?
The fat melts out and the skin turns crisp
The meat soaks up fat and gets richer
The skin stays soft and easy to remove
The juices rise up into the skin
This is called rendering: a thick layer of fat becomes a thin, crisp skin and the pan fills with duck fat.
A cook “bastes” a steak (in French: arroser). What does that mean?
Spooning the hot pan butter over it
Rubbing cold butter in before cooking
Injecting melted butter into the centre
Foaming butter with garlic and thyme is spooned over again and again: it browns the crust and adds flavour.
What is a “French-trimmed” rack of lamb?
The ends of the rib bones are scraped clean
All the rib bones have been taken out
The fat cap is left on, extra thick
The meat is sliced into thin escalopes
The clean white bones are for looks, and they make a neat “handle” on each cutlet.
Raw meat or fish, finely chopped and seasoned
Raw meat or fish, cut in paper-thin slices
Raw fish, cured in citrus juice
Cooked meat, shredded in its own fat
Beef tartare is the classic, often with a raw egg yolk. Always tell the guest that it is raw.
Raw meat or fish in paper-thin slices
Raw meat or fish, finely chopped
Cooked meat, pressed in a mould
Fish cured in salt, sugar and dill
The original, from Harry’s Bar in Venice, is raw beef. Today the word is used for anything sliced very thin.
What “cooks” the fish in a ceviche?
A bath of warm olive oil
Lime juice firms the flesh and turns it opaque, but there is no heat: for the guest it is still raw fish.
A mixture pressed in a mould, served in slices
A clear soup served in a small cup
A stew baked under a lid of pastry
A warm mousse piped onto slices of toast
Named after the earthenware dish it is cooked in. It can be meat, fish or vegetables and is served cold.
Meat cooked slowly in fat, shredded to a spread
Thin slices of air-dried cured ham
A smooth mousse of liver and cream
Pork, duck or rabbit, served cold with bread. Coarser and more fibrous than a pâté.
Which milk is Parmigiano Reggiano made from?
Parmigiano Reggiano is a hard cow’s-milk cheese from northern Italy, aged for a year or more until grainy and savoury.
Which milk is Roquefort made from?
Roquefort is a French blue cheese from raw sheep’s milk, ripened in the caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon.
The Italian cheeses called Pecorino are all made from…
Pecora is Italian for sheep: Pecorino Romano, Sardo and Toscano are all sheep’s-milk cheeses.
On a French cheese board, “chèvre” means a cheese made from…
Chèvre is French for goat. These cheeses are usually white, tangy and fresh, often shaped as small logs.
Manchego is a firm sheep’s-milk cheese from La Mancha in central Spain, often served with quince paste.
Which of these is a blue cheese?
Gorgonzola is a cow’s-milk blue from northern Italy: dolce is young and creamy, piccante older and sharper.
Stilton, the blue cheese served with port, comes from…
Stilton is the classic English blue, made from cow’s milk: crumbly, rich and less salty than Roquefort.
Comté is a hard cow’s-milk cheese from the Jura mountains in eastern France: nutty, and sweeter with age.
What makes the blue-green veins in a blue cheese?
A mould added to the milk or curd
Dried herbs mixed into the curd
The mould is Penicillium. The cheese is pierced with needles so air gets in and the veins can grow.
Why does a washed-rind cheese like Taleggio have an orange rind and a strong smell?
Its rind is washed with brine as it ripens
It is smoked over beech wood
It is rolled in ground paprika
It is aged wrapped in vine leaves
Washing feeds bacteria that colour the rind and give the smell. The inside is usually much milder than the nose suggests.
The soft white rind of Brie and Camembert is…
It is a “bloomy” rind of Penicillium candidum. It is meant to be eaten and adds a mushroomy note.
Burrata is a pouch of mozzarella filled with stracciatella. Serve it at room temperature so the centre runs.
Curd pressed and kept in brine
Ricotta means “recooked”: the whey is heated again until fine, sweet curds rise. Bulgarian izvara is a close cousin.
Halloumi is the traditional cheese of which island?
Halloumi is a firm, salty Cypriot cheese of sheep’s and goat’s milk, often flavoured with a little mint.
Why can halloumi be grilled in slices?
It holds its shape and does not melt
It is coated in flour beforehand
It is aged until rock hard
The curd is heated in whey during making, so the cheese only softens and browns on the grill. It squeaks when you bite it.
How is Bulgarian white sirene ripened?
Hung up to dry in the air
The brine is why sirene is salty, moist and crumbly. It is made from cow’s, sheep’s, goat’s or buffalo milk.
A white cheese kept in brine
Kashkaval is a stretched-curd cheese, a cousin of Italian caciocavallo, made from cow’s or sheep’s milk.
A thick, salty fermented milk spread
A dried mix of herbs and salt
A relish of peppers and tomatoes
Katak is traditionally made from late-summer sheep’s milk: tangy, salty and thick enough to spread on bread.
Thick cream skimmed from heated milk
Yoghurt hung to drain in a cloth
Kaymak is the rich clotted cream of the Balkans and Turkey, served fresh or lightly aged with grilled meat and bread.
Labneh comes from the Levant. It is as thick as cream cheese and is served with olive oil and za’atar.
Mascarpone is cream thickened with a little acid, which is why it is so rich. It is the base of tiramisù.
The crunchy white specks in a long-aged Parmigiano are…
They are tyrosine crystals that form as the proteins break down: a sign of long ripening, not a fault.
What does rennet do in cheesemaking?
Rennet is an enzyme, traditionally from a calf’s stomach, that splits milk into curds and whey.
A “raw-milk” cheese is made from milk that has not been…
Raw milk keeps more of the farm’s own flavour. Parmigiano Reggiano, Roquefort and Comté are all raw-milk cheeses.
Gouda is named after a Dutch town. Young it is mild and supple; aged it turns hard, with caramel notes.
In the EU, the name “feta” is reserved for cheese from…
Feta is a protected Greek name for brined cheese from sheep’s milk with some goat’s. Ours is called sirene.
Which of these is a washed-rind cheese?
Époisses from Burgundy is washed with marc brandy as it ripens: sticky orange rind, powerful smell, creamy heart.
Which cheese is made by stretching the hot curd?
This is “pasta filata”, spun curd: it is stretched in hot water. Provolone and kashkaval are made the same way.
As a hard cheese ages, it becomes…
Drier, firmer and stronger in taste
Water evaporates and proteins and fats break down, so the flavour concentrates. That is why aged cheeses cost more.
Bulgarian yoghurt is made with Lactobacillus bulgaricus and…
The two bacteria work together. The others are the mould of blue cheese, baker’s yeast and the koji mould.
Prosciutto crudo is made from which part of the pig?
The leg is salted and air-dried for many months. Parma and San Daniele are the best-known Italian ones.
Bresaola comes from Valtellina in the Italian Alps: lean, dark red and sliced paper-thin, often with rocket and Parmigiano.
A fresh sausage for the grill
Lukanka is minced pork and beef with cumin and black pepper, pressed flat as it dries. Slice it thin, at an angle.
Pastarma is meat that has been…
Minced and stuffed in a casing
Cooked slowly in its own fat
It is usually beef. The Turkish and Armenian style is coated in chemen, a spicy paste of fenugreek, garlic and paprika.
Guanciale is cured pork from which part of the pig?
Guancia is Italian for cheek. Guanciale is fattier and richer than pancetta, which is cured belly.
What gives Spanish chorizo its red colour?
Pimentón, Spanish paprika, sweet or hot and often smoked, colours and flavours every chorizo.
How does speck from Alto Adige differ from prosciutto di Parma?
Speck joins two traditions: salted and air-dried as in the south, smoked as in the north of the Alps.
Elenski but, Bulgaria’s dry-cured ham, takes its name from…
It is a pork leg salted and dried for months in the mountain air around Elena, in the central Balkan Mountains.
True caviar is the salted roe of which fish?
Roe from salmon or trout is sold under the name of the fish. Only sturgeon roe is called simply “caviar”.
Which sturgeon caviar has the largest eggs?
Beluga is the biggest sturgeon and gives large, soft, grey pearls. Sevruga has the smallest eggs of the classic three.
Salted, pressed and dried fish roe
It is made from grey mullet or tuna roe in Sardinia and Sicily, and grated over pasta like a salty, savoury cheese.
On a Japanese menu, ikura is the roe of…
Ikura are large orange salmon eggs that pop in the mouth. The tiny crunchy ones are tobiko, from flying fish.
On a Japanese menu, uni is…
Uni is the soft orange roe of the sea urchin: creamy, sweet and briny. Unagi, which sounds similar, is freshwater eel.
Which of these is a flat fish?
Turbot, the kalkan of the Black Sea, lies on the seabed with both eyes on one side. Sole and halibut are flat fish too.
Which of these is an oily fish?
Oily fish carry their fat in the flesh: mackerel, sardines, herring, salmon. White fish like cod are lean and mild.
Octopus, squid and cuttlefish belong to which group?
Cephalopod means “head-foot”. They are molluscs with no outer shell, and all three carry ink.
In Japanese cuisine, toro is which part of a tuna?
Toro is pale, rich and melting. Otoro is the fattiest part, chutoro is medium, and the lean red meat is akami.
Bacalhau in Portugal and baccalà in Italy are…
The cod is salted and dried so it keeps for months, then soaked in water for a day or two before cooking.
Which cut of beef is the most tender?
The fillet, or tenderloin, does almost no work, so it is very tender and lean, but milder in flavour than ribeye or sirloin.
A T-bone steak has which two cuts on either side of the bone?
The T-shaped bone separates the two. A porterhouse is the same cut with a larger piece of fillet.
Wagyu are Japanese cattle breeds, above all Japanese Black, known for intense marbling and soft, buttery fat.
Kobe beef is wagyu from which Japanese prefecture?
Kobe is the capital of Hyogo. Only Tajima-strain cattle born and raised there can be sold as Kobe beef.
The thymus gland of a calf or lamb
The kidneys of a calf or lamb
The brain of a calf or lamb
The testicles of a calf or lamb
Sweetbreads come only from young animals. They are pale, delicate and creamy, usually pan-fried until golden.
The fattened liver of a duck or goose
The breast of a fattened duck
The rendered fat of a goose
Foie gras is French for “fat liver”. It is rich and buttery, and is usually served with something sweet or sharp.
Strictly, magret is the breast of a duck fattened for foie gras: thick, dark and served pink like a steak.
Which of these is a game bird?
Game is wild or hunted meat: pheasant, partridge, deer, wild boar. It is lean, with a deeper flavour than farmed meat.
Onglet, or hanger steak, comes from which part of the animal?
It “hangs” from the diaphragm near the kidneys: loose-grained and dark, with a strong beefy taste. Best served rare.
Which herb is the heart of sharena sol, Bulgaria’s “colourful salt”?
Sharena sol is salt mixed with dried savory (chubritsa), paprika and fenugreek. It is served with bread for dipping.
Middle-Eastern tahini is a paste made from…
The seeds are toasted and ground until runny. Tahini is nutty and slightly bitter, and goes into hummus and many sauces.
Sumac is a dark red powder of dried berries, sprinkled over salads, grilled meat and yoghurt for a fresh, sharp note.
The blend za’atar is sesame seeds, sumac and…
The herb itself is also called za’atar, a wild relative of thyme and oregano. The blend goes on bread, labneh and vegetables.
Pomegranate juice boiled down to a syrup
It is thick, dark and sweet-sour, used across the Middle East in dressings, glazes and marinades.
A chilli paste from North Africa
Harissa is Tunisian: dried chillies pounded with garlic, caraway, coriander and olive oil. Tell guests it is hot.
Picked green and roasted over fire
The young grains are scorched in the field, which gives freekeh its smoky, nutty taste and a firm bite.
Miso is a fermented paste of…
Soybeans are fermented with salt and koji for months. White miso is mild and sweet, red miso darker and saltier.
Kombu seaweed is prized in Japanese cooking as a natural source of…
Kombu is dried kelp, rich in natural glutamate. Umami was first identified in it, in Japan, in 1908.
Japanese katsuobushi flakes are shaved from…
Katsuobushi, or bonito flakes, is skipjack tuna dried until hard as wood, then shaved paper-thin.
Yuzu tastes between lemon, mandarin and grapefruit. Mostly the juice and zest are used, in sauces, desserts and cocktails.
Ponzu is a Japanese sauce built on soy sauce and…
Ponzu is tart and salty: yuzu or another citrus with soy, mirin and dashi. It goes with raw fish, seared meat and dumplings.
A mould grown on steamed rice
A yeast that makes beer foam
An alga dried into thin sheets
Koji (Aspergillus oryzae) turns starch and protein into sugar and umami. Sake, miso and soy sauce all start with it.
A sweet rice wine for cooking
A sour rice vinegar for sushi
A salty sauce of fermented fish
A hot oil of toasted sesame
Mirin gives Japanese sauces and glazes their gentle sweetness and shine, as in teriyaki.
Real wasabi is the grated stem of a plant related to…
Wasabi grows in cold running water and is costly. Most “wasabi” paste is really horseradish and mustard, coloured green.
Panko flakes are larger and airier than ordinary breadcrumbs, so the coating fries up lighter and crunchier.
Korean grilled beef in soy sauce
Cabbage is salted, rubbed with chilli, garlic and ginger and left to ferment: sour, spicy and a little fizzy.
It is made from chilli, sticky rice and fermented soybeans: hot, sweet and savoury at once.
Saffron comes from which part of a plant?
The stigmas of a crocus flower
The bark of a tropical tree
The root of a ginger relative
Each flower gives only three threads, picked by hand. That is why saffron costs so much. It colours food golden.
A vanilla pod is the fruit of…
The green pods of the vanilla orchid are cured for months until black and fragrant. Tiny black seeds are a sign of real vanilla.
The town of Alba in Piedmont is famous for which ingredient?
White truffles are found there in autumn. They are shaved raw over the warm dish at the table, never cooked.
Which of these mushrooms is still only gathered wild, not farmed?
Porcini (ceps) live in partnership with tree roots, so they cannot be farmed. That is why they are seasonal and often sold dried.
It grows covered with soil, away from light
It is a different, colourless species
It is peeled and soaked in lemon water
It is picked only after the first frost
Without light the spears make no chlorophyll. They are milder than green asparagus and are always peeled.
What does “extra virgin” mean on a bottle of olive oil?
Top grade: only pressed, never refined
Light grade: filtered to a mild taste
Second pressing of the olive pulp
Olive oil blended with seed oil
Extra virgin oil is simply the juice of fresh olives, with the lowest acidity: fruity, a little bitter and peppery.
Traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena is made from…
The must is aged for at least 12 years in a row of ever smaller wooden barrels until thick, dark and sweet-sour.
Sea salt skimmed from the surface of salt pans
Rock salt mined deep in the mountains
Table salt smoked over oak wood
Sea salt mixed with dried flowers
“Flower of salt” forms as a thin crust on calm, sunny days. It is a finishing salt, sprinkled on at the end.
What does white chocolate contain from the cocoa bean?
White chocolate is cocoa butter, sugar and milk with no cocoa solids: that is why it is ivory and tastes of milk and vanilla.
Mace is the lacy red covering of which spice?
Both come from one fruit: nutmeg is the seed and mace the web around it, similar in taste but finer and lighter.
Besides soy, which allergen is in ordinary soy sauce?
Classic soy sauce is brewed from soybeans and wheat. Tamari is the version usually made without wheat.
Which allergen hides in Worcestershire sauce?
It is made with fermented anchovies, so it is not vegetarian either. It turns up in dressings, marinades and Bloody Mary.
Marzipan is made from sugar and which nut?
Marzipan is ground almonds and sugar, so a cake covered or filled with it is not for a guest with a nut allergy.
Which allergen is in classic hummus?
Hummus is chickpeas blended with tahini, and tahini is ground sesame. Baba ghanoush has it too.
Surimi “crab sticks” are made mainly from…
Surimi is minced white fish shaped and flavoured like crab, so the allergen is fish. It often has egg white and wheat too.
Which allergen is always in real mayonnaise?
Mayonnaise is egg yolk and oil, often with mustard. It has no dairy, though many guests think it does.
Which allergen hides in most classic vinaigrettes?
A spoon of mustard holds the oil and vinegar together, so dressings, marinades and many sauces carry this allergen.
Which allergen is in almost every classic stock and soup base?
Celery goes into the classic vegetable base with onion and carrot, so sauces and soups carry it even when you cannot see it.
Besides wine, which food very often contains sulphites?
Sulphites keep dried fruit bright and stop it browning. Vinegar and some pickles contain them as well.
Lupin is one of the 14 allergens. What kind of plant is it?
A nut tree, related to almonds
Lupin flour and seeds turn up in bread, pastry and gluten-free products. Guests allergic to peanuts may react to it.
Which of these is a mollusc, not a crustacean?
Molluscs are squid, octopus, mussels, oysters and clams. Crustaceans have legs and a jointed shell: prawns, crabs, lobsters.
Under which of the 14 allergens do snails (escargots) fall?
Land snails are molluscs, just like mussels and squid, and are declared under the same allergen.
A legume, like beans and peas
A tree nut, like the walnut
Peanuts grow in pods under the ground, which is why they are declared separately from tree nuts.
Which of these counts as a tree nut in the list of 14 allergens?
The tree nuts are almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, cashews, pecans, Brazil nuts, pistachios and macadamias.
Taramasalata must be flagged for which allergy?
Tarama is cured fish roe whipped with bread, oil and lemon. Roe counts as fish, and the bread adds gluten.
Bulgur and couscous are both made from…
Both are wheat, so tabbouleh or a couscous garnish is not for a coeliac guest.
Which of these grains contains gluten?
Gluten is in wheat, rye and barley. Rice, maize and buckwheat are naturally free of it.
Which of these is naturally gluten-free?
Quinoa, rice, maize and millet have no gluten. In the kitchen they must still be kept well away from flour.
Spelt and einkorn are old varieties of which grain?
They are ancient wheats and contain gluten, so einkorn bread is not for a coeliac guest, whatever people say about it.
Lactose intolerance is trouble digesting this sugar. A milk allergy is a reaction to milk proteins and is far more dangerous.
Which dairy product has almost no lactose?
During long ageing the bacteria use up the lactose. It is still milk, so it is never right for a milk allergy.
Why is lactose-free milk unsafe for a guest with a milk allergy?
It still has the milk proteins
It still has traces of lactose
An allergy is to the proteins, an intolerance to the sugar. Always ask the guest which of the two they mean.
Which system of the body reacts in a true food allergy?
That is why an allergy can become life-threatening within minutes, while an intolerance is unpleasant but rarely dangerous.
How much of an allergen can set off a serious reaction?
A trace too small to see
A crumb, a used spoon or a splash of sauce can be enough, which is why “just pick it off” is never an answer.
Prawns were fried in the oil before the chips. What happens to their allergen?
It sinks and is strained out
Heat does not remove allergens. Food fried in shared oil is not safe for the allergic guest: tell the kitchen.
In allergen safety, what is cross-contact?
An allergen gets into another food by accident
Two guests share one dish at the table
One dish contains two different allergens
A guest is allergic to two different foods
It happens through shared boards, oil, spoons, hands and cloths, and the dish looks perfectly normal.
A dish for a guest with a nut allergy reaches the pass with nuts on top. What now?
Ask the kitchen for a new dish
Serve it and warn the guest
Ask a cook to scrape them off
Once the allergen has touched the food, traces stay. Only a dish made again from the start is safe.
A guest says: “I am only slightly allergic, don’t make a fuss.” What do you do?
Tell the kitchen all the same
Let it go, as the guest asked
Note it only if they insist
Every allergy goes on the order and to the kitchen, however mild it sounds. The kitchen has the last word.
How do you put down the dish made specially for a guest with an allergy?
Saying what it was made without
In the middle, for the guest to take
“Your risotto, made without nuts” tells the guest the message reached the kitchen and stops plates being mixed up.
How is gluten-free bread brought to a coeliac guest?
On its own plate, apart from other bread
In the shared basket, on top
In the shared basket, in a napkin
On a board with the other bread
Crumbs of ordinary bread are enough to make a coeliac guest ill, so the bread never shares a basket, board or knife.
A guest’s lips swell and they struggle to breathe after eating. What do you do first?
Bring water and wait a little
Offer a pill from the staff room
Walk the guest out for fresh air
These are signs of a severe allergic reaction and minutes matter. 112 is the emergency number everywhere in the EU.
Which of these is not vegan?
Vegans avoid everything that comes from animals: not only meat and fish but also eggs, dairy, gelatine and honey.
What does a vegetarian eat that a vegan does not?
A vegetarian eats no meat or fish but usually does eat eggs, milk and cheese. A vegan eats only plant foods.
What does a pescatarian guest eat?
Fish and seafood, but no meat
Meat, but no fish or seafood
Pescatarians skip meat and poultry but eat fish, and usually eggs and dairy too. Mind the stock: no chicken or veal.
It comes mostly from pork and beef, so a panna cotta, jelly or mousse set with it is not vegetarian.
Traditional rennet, used for many hard cheeses, comes from…
That is why Parmesan and many classic hard cheeses are not strictly vegetarian. Ask the kitchen which cheeses are.
What makes a classic Caesar dressing unsuitable for vegetarians?
Anchovies, or the Worcestershire sauce that contains them, give the dressing its savoury depth. For allergies it is fish.
Classic Japanese dashi stock is not vegetarian because it contains…
Dashi is kombu seaweed and katsuobushi, dried smoked fish. It is the base of miso soup and of many Japanese sauces.
A guest keeps halal. Which pair is ruled out?
That covers bacon, lard and pork gelatine, and wine or spirits in sauces and desserts. Other meat must be halal.
Which combination is not allowed in a kosher meal?
Kosher rules keep meat and milk apart: no butter or cream sauce on meat and no cheese in the same course.
Which of these can never be kosher?
Kosher seafood must have fins and scales, so prawns, crab, mussels and squid are all out. So is pork.
Why do your fingers never touch the rim of a guest’s glass?
Hold a glass by the stem or base, cutlery by the handle, a plate by its edge: never where the mouth or the food goes.
A guest drops a fork on the floor. What do you do?
Bring a clean one at once
Wipe it and hand it back
Put it back on the table
Bring the clean fork first, on a plate or a napkin, then pick up the dropped one and wash your hands.
You had vomiting or diarrhoea this morning. What do you do about your shift?
Tell the manager and stay away from food
Work as usual, but wear gloves
Work, but carry only the drinks
Take a pill and say nothing
A stomach bug passes very easily to guests through plates, glasses and hands, even when you already feel better.
You cut your finger during service. What do you do before going back to the floor?
Clean it and cover it with a waterproof plaster
Rinse it and let it dry in the open air
Wrap it tightly in a paper napkin
Press it with your service cloth
An open cut carries bacteria onto plates and glasses. A covered one protects both the guest and you.
What is the waiter’s cloth never used for?
Catching a drip from a bottle
Wiping the neck of a bottle
The cloth touches plates and bottles that go to the guest, so it stays spotless and is changed as soon as it is marked.
A small bite from the kitchen before the meal
A sorbet served between two courses
Small sweets served with the coffee
A plate of cheese before the dessert
It is the chef’s greeting: not ordered and not charged. Say what it is, and check the table’s allergies before it goes out.
In a classic menu, where does the fish course come?
A classic menu builds from light to rich: cold starter, soup, fish, then meat.
Why is a small sorbet sometimes served between two savoury courses?
The cold and the acidity clear away the taste of the previous dish, so the next one tastes clean.
With the coffee, at the end
With the aperitif, at the start
With the bread, before the starter
They are tiny sweets and chocolates, the last taste the guest takes away, usually with the compliments of the house.
What does ordering “à la carte” mean?
Each dish is chosen and priced separately
The chef chooses the dishes for the table
A set menu is served at one fixed price
All dishes are shared in the middle
The opposite is a set or tasting menu, where the courses and the price are fixed in advance.
What does “mise en place” mean on the floor?
Everything set and ready before service
The last check of a plate at the pass
The seating plan for the evening
The clearing of a table after guests
Polished glasses and cutlery, folded napkins, stocked stations: what is ready before service does not slow you during it.
In restaurant language, what is a “cover”?
The lid of a serving dish
The folder that holds the bill
The word also counts guests: “forty covers tonight” means forty people served.
A dome that covers a plate until it is served
A trolley for carving beside the table
A stand that holds the wine bucket
A small bell for calling the waiter
At a table all the cloches are lifted at the same moment, so every guest sees the dish hot and at its best.
In which order does a guest use the cutlery laid at the place?
So you lay the cutlery for the first course furthest from the plate, and that for the main course next to it.
Which way does the blade of a table knife face?
Knives lie on the right with the blade turned in towards the plate, forks on the left with the tines up.
On which side of the cover does the bread plate stand?
On the left, beside the forks
On the right, beside the knives
On the right, below the glasses
In the centre, above the plate
Bread on the left, drinks on the right. That is why bread is offered from the guest’s left and drinks from the right.
Where do the glasses stand in a place setting?
On the right, above the knife
On the left, above the forks
On the left, by the bread plate
In the centre, above the plate
The first glass stands above the tip of the main knife, within easy reach of the right hand.
Where is the dessert cutlery laid when it is on the table from the start?
On the far right, outside the knives
On the far left, outside the forks
On the bread plate, side by side
Before dessert you slide them down to the sides: the spoon to the right, the fork to the left.
What is the broad, blunt fish knife made to do?
Lift the flesh off the bones
Cooked fish is tender and needs no cutting edge. The flat blade slides between flesh, skin and bone.
A decorative base plate, not eaten from
A sharing platter for the middle of the table
A small side plate for bread and butter
A warmed plate for the main course
It dresses the empty place while the guests sit down. Food is never put directly on it.
At a table in classic service, who is served last?
The host invited the others and looks after them, so everyone else is served before the person who booked the table.
In classic service, in which order are the guests at a table served?
The classic order starts with the guest of honour or the eldest lady, then the other ladies, then the gentlemen.
From which side is food served from a platter with spoon and fork (silver service)?
The platter rests on your left arm and your right hand serves, so from the left you never cross the guest.
A dish is finished on a trolley by the table
Every plate arrives under a dome
Guests help themselves from a buffet
All dishes come at once, to share
The gueridon is the small side table or trolley for carving, filleting, flambéing or dressing a salad in front of the guest.
In the classic dining-room brigade, what does a chef de rang do?
Runs a station of several tables
Above him is the maître d’hôtel, below him the commis who carries and clears. The “rang” is his group of tables.
A guest lays knife and fork side by side on the plate. What does it mean?
Knife and fork together, parallel, is the sign that the plate may go, once everyone at the table has finished.
Knife and fork rest apart on the plate, tips towards each other. What is the guest saying?
I would like the next course
Open or crossed cutlery means a pause. Leave the plate, even if the guest has stepped away for a moment.
When do you clear the plates of a course?
When everyone at the table has finished
As soon as each guest has finished
When the next course is ready
Taking one plate early hurries those still eating and leaves the first guest sitting at an empty place.
When is the table crumbed down?
After the main course, before dessert
While the main course is eaten
Only after the guests have left
With a crumber or a folded napkin you brush the crumbs onto a small plate, never onto the floor or into your hand.
What leaves the table together with the main-course plates, before dessert?
Everything that belongs to the savoury part goes: salt and pepper, bread, butter and side plates. Then the crumbs.
Why do you repeat the order back to the table before you leave?
To catch a mistake before the kitchen starts
To give the guests time to add some wine
To show the guests that you remember it
To let the guests hear the prices again
Ten seconds at the table cost less than a wrong dish: confirm the dishes, how the meat is cooked, and any allergy.
Why do you write each order against the guest’s seat number?
So each plate reaches its guest without asking
So the kitchen cooks the dishes in seat order
So the guests keep the same seats all evening
So each dish is priced by where the guest sits
Asking “who has the fish?” at the table tells the guests that nobody was listening when they ordered.
What do you ask every table before you take the food order?
How long they plan to stay
Who will be paying the bill
How much they wish to spend
Ask before the order, not after it: the kitchen can then say what is safe and what can be changed.
A dish is sold out tonight. When do the guests hear about it?
When you hand them the menus
When they try to order it
When the kitchen sends the order back
When the other dishes are served
“I am sorry, that is finished” after the guest has chosen is a small disappointment you can spare them.
How do the dishes of one course reach a table of six?
Each one as soon as it is ready
Hot dishes first, cold ones after
Two at a time, minutes apart
Nobody should watch the others eat. If you cannot carry them all, a colleague walks with you and the plates land together.
When do you check that the guests are happy with a dish?
The moment you put it down
By then they have tasted it, and anything wrong can still be put right while the rest of the table is eating.
When do you change a guest’s cutlery for the next course?
As you put the dish down
After the guest asks for it
A guest with a hot plate and no knife cannot start. Check every cover against the order before the food leaves the pass.
How do you carry clean cutlery to a table where guests are seated?
On a plate lined with a napkin
In your hand, by the handles
In the pocket of your apron
The napkin stops the cutlery sliding and rattling, and your fingers stay off it in front of the guest.
Where is the soup spoon laid?
On the right, with the knives
On the left, with the forks
On the bread plate, on the left
Spoons and knives lie on the right, forks on the left. Only the dessert cutlery lies above the plate.
A plate has the house crest on its rim. Where does the crest sit when you put it down?
At the top, furthest from the guest
At the bottom, nearest the guest
On the left, towards the forks
On the right, towards the knives
The crest sits at twelve o’clock, and the dish faces the guest the way the chef plated it, the same at every place.
When do you bring a finger bowl?
With food eaten with the fingers
Shellfish in the shell, artichoke or asparagus: warm water with a slice of lemon, and a fresh napkin beside it.
A soft felt cloth under the tablecloth
A small napkin wrapped round a bottle
A square cloth laid over the tablecloth
A long cloth that covers the sideboard
It deadens the sound of plates and glasses, protects the table top and keeps the tablecloth from slipping.
What does “full hands in, full hands out” mean?
Carry as many plates as you can hold
Always hold one plate with both hands
Bring every drink on a full tray
Food or drinks go out, and something always comes back: an empty glass, a finished plate, a used napkin.
A guest starts to complain about a dish. What do you do first?
Listen to the end without interrupting
Explain how the dish is meant to be
Fetch the chef to the table
Listen, apologise, put it right, then tell the manager. Explaining or arguing sounds like “you are wrong”.
The kitchen is running well behind for one of your tables. What do you do?
Tell the guests before they have to ask
Stay away until the food is ready
Say that it is just about to arrive
